## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can an agent lose the thread of a task even when its entire history still fits?_

An agent context window is a finite, expensive operating system memory space, not an unbounded repository for raw text. Naively accumulating tool outputs, conversational turns, and retrieval snippets rapidly exhausts token capacity, inflates prompt prefill latency, and degrades the model attention distribution over critical task instructions. Effective context engineering treats the prompt as an active working register: relevant state must be aggressively compressed, irrelevant observations evicted, and volatile workspace artifacts externalized to persistent datastores. Stale evidence or truncated tool records in context directly induce model hallucinations that cascade across downstream turns. The systems challenge is maintaining an authoritative, minimal projection of environment truth within the token budget, ensuring that carried state actively bounds trajectory uncertainty rather than compounding it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Distinguish nominal request capacity from usable working context and explain why admitted tokens dilute needed evidence
- Allocate the next request's input budget while preserving output headroom and task-relevant evidence
- Design a context layout that separates source roles from change rate and supports compatible prefix reuse
- Compare compaction policies by information loss, recovery requirements, and the cost of repeated transformations
- Audit a progress record against runtime-owned sources and price the protected-field check that preserves constraints
- Apply dependency-aware invalidation without treating historical observations as proof of current state
- Evaluate context policies by decision quality, accepted outcomes, and total resource use under common limits

:::
## Carrying a Repair Across Turns {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-overview}

The repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) has spent several turns investigating a connection-pool defect. It has inspected the pool implementation, executed a reproduction test, and revised its initial diagnosis. None of that hard-won progress lives inside the model. Because foundation models are stateless functions across turns, every call begins and ends with the payload assembled by the host runtime. The agent can use the test trace, honor public API constraints, and avoid revisiting a rejected hypothesis only if the runtime includes them in the upcoming request, structured so that the status and role of each artifact remain unambiguous.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with only the State axis lit in purple."}

*This chapter develops State through the selection, representation, and refresh of working context.*
:::

The token accounting of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-tokenization resolves a basic operational constraint for an individual request: whether the payload satisfies the admission bound. Yet accounting bounds do not dictate semantic utility. A prompt can fit well within token limits and still fail to guide the agent toward a valid repair. The simplest agent architectures evade this problem by treating context as an append-only log, concatenating every observation, tool execution, and partial response into an expanding transcript. That policy breaks down almost immediately. Even while the transcript fits within physical limits, the runtime pays repeatedly for obsolete tokens that the next decision no longer requires. Stale code snippets sit alongside their replacements, and refuted hypotheses linger alongside the test results that disproved them, diluting the model's attention. When an extended trajectory inevitably exhausts the context window, an unmanaged runtime is forced into blind truncation, evicting vital instructions or early constraints without any principled criteria for what to preserve.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The quadratic input cost of resending an append-only history on every call is established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-trajectory-cost-accumulation.
:::

This chapter develops the agent's *working context*: the runtime subsystem that decides what each model call receives. Rather than treating context as a passive transcript, this subsystem constructs a bounded working set tailored to a single decision. It establishes token budgets for each distinct role in the prompt, arranges data layouts so unchanged prefixes can be reused across turns, compacts historical evidence without corrupting its factual validity, maintains structured progress records that resist summarization drift, and enforces invalidation rules whenever external actions alter environment state. All of these mechanisms run as deterministic host software. The foundation model reasons over the assembled working context, but the host runtime remains solely responsible for managing it.

Tracing the repair agent through its next decision reveals how these systems components operate in concert. The runtime first formulates the working-set decision (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision), identifying the minimal sufficient evidence required for the next step and partitioning the input token allowance across competing roles. This allocation cannot simply mirror vendor-specified context windows. Measured context capacity (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics) demonstrates a sharp divergence between the raw token limits an API accepts and the narrower bounds within which a model reliably attends to dense evidence. Once selected, context items require disciplined staging (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging). The runtime structures prompts to establish clear data provenance, maintain role boundaries, and stabilize shared prefixes so that multi-turn interactions can exploit key-value caching in the serving engine. As extended troubleshooting stretches the step budget, compaction (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction) reduces history to its essential results, while structured progress records (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-summarization) preserve critical decisions and refuted hypotheses without the informational drift typical of free-form text summarization. Furthermore, because tool executions mutate the surrounding software environment, active invalidation policies (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot) withdraw obsolete observations before they can mislead downstream reasoning. Finally, rigorous context evaluation (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation) tests whether the assembled context policy reliably guides the agent to correct defect repairs while controlling end-to-end latency and dollar cost.

## The Working-Set Decision {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-decision}

As our connection-pool investigation unfolds, the runtime accumulates far more information than was present at initialization. A controlled test has demonstrated that a connection returned to the pool while a waiting client remained blocked. Consequently, the initial timeout hypothesis has been undermined, leaving missed notification as the leading candidate explanation. The next model invocation must capitalize on this empirical progress. If the runtime blindly replays the entire conversational history without distinguishing raw observations from superseded hypotheses, it forces the model to re-evaluate discounted failure modes alongside the very evidence that disproved them.

Consider the state of the codebase at version `r17`, where the relevant files are `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py`, and the failure is captured by the reproducer `test_waiter_notified_on_return`. Before prompting the model for a candidate patch, the runtime must determine precisely which source excerpts, empirical test results, architectural constraints, and unresolved questions are required in the upcoming prompt. We call this choice the **working-set decision**\index{Working-set decision!definition}\index{Context engineering!working-set decision}: the runtime must select the bounded subset of task information necessary to execute the next concrete step.

The term draws inspiration from Denning's classic working-set model of program behavior [@denning1968].\index{Working set!Denning model} Over any temporal window, an executing program references only a fraction of its total address space. By keeping this active working set resident in physical page frames, an operating system avoids thrashing while relegating dormant pages to backing storage. An agent runtime faces an analogous residency challenge: it must stage the right tokens in context to support the immediate operation without exhausting its prompt budget. Yet an essential architectural divergence distinguishes context engineering from virtual memory. Denning's working set is measured dynamically from page references the program has already issued. An agent runtime, by contrast, must construct the context working set *before* issuing the model call, relying on a predictive judgment about what the upcoming decision will require.[^fn-belady-optimal-replacement] Furthermore, standard foundation model interfaces report only generated tokens; they emit no hardware-style reference bits or access telemetry to indicate which staged context tokens the model actually utilized during inference.

[^fn-belady-optimal-replacement]: **Optimal Replacement (MIN)**: @belady1966study evaluated page-replacement algorithms against an optimal offline baseline that evicts the page whose next reference lies farthest in the future. Practical operating systems approximate this unrealizable clairvoyance using historical access patterns such as least recently used (LRU). An agent context runtime lacks even that access history: because the model interface reports no reference bits for the tokens it processes, working-set selection must rely on explicit domain heuristics and structured task state rather than on observed cache reuse. \index{Belady optimal replacement!context selection}

In context management, relevance must govern selection rather than chronological recency. Core user constraints established at the start of a session remain binding after dozens of intermediate tool invocations, whereas a lengthy test log generated moments ago may offer only a single diagnostic status code. Moreover, candidate information extends far beyond the linear dialogue history. System instructions, schema declarations for available tools, newly inspected source files, and dynamically retrieved reference documents [@lewis2020retrieval] all compete for space in the assembled request. The runtime must synthesize an operational representation from these disparate sources, adhering strictly to the principle of source authority: the physical environment remains the sole authority on system state, and runtime policies govern what actions are permissible (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}).

To structure this selection, the runtime compiles a **context manifest**\index{Context manifest!definition}—a structured inventory that enumerates each artifact designated for the upcoming request alongside the rationale for its inclusion. The manifest for the connection-pool repair's next request (@tbl-vol3-context-manifest) reads as an architectural specification rather than a raw byte serialization: each row names an entry and the content the next step needs from it. Artifacts such as code snippets and test logs are itemized with their contextual provenance, ensuring that their substantive contents are injected only where directly relevant to the pending decision.

| Selected entry          | Content needed for the next step                                                                                                                                            |
|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Goal and constraints    | Repair waiter notification; preserve the public API; remain within the approved workspace; do not deploy to production.                                                     |
| Current artifacts       | Relevant source and test excerpts from `src/pool.py` and `tests/test_pool.py` at `r17`, together with the configuration used by the controlled test.                        |
| Observed result         | On `r17`, the controlled waiter/return test recorded an available connection while a waiter remained blocked. Keep the test identity and conditions attached to the result. |
| Hypothesis status       | The timeout explanation has lost support. Missed notification remains a hypothesis, not an established cause.                                                               |
| Repair and check status | No candidate patch has yet been checked. Behavior outside the controlled reproducer remains unresolved.                                                                     |
| Next bounded step       | Propose a candidate change to the notification path using the current excerpts; do not report the defect as repaired.                                                       |

: **Selecting the next request**: Each entry supplies a distinct part of the illustrative connection-pool decision. Version labels identify the example’s artifacts, not measured repository revisions. {#tbl-vol3-context-manifest tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Curating this manifest demands disciplined relevance filtering. Retaining an empirical failure log without binding it to its source commit (`r17`) risks contaminating later turns, where an obsolete error trace might be mistaken for evidence against a newly patched implementation. Similarly, recording an abbreviated label like "notification bug" without qualifying its uncertainty prematurely elevates a working hypothesis to an established root cause. Conversely, retaining the full conversational history of rejected theories wastes valuable context capacity; once the runtime records that the timeout hypothesis was refuted by specific test evidence, the multi-turn deliberations that led to that hypothesis can be safely discarded. While a foundation model can assist in summarizing past turns to build this representation, the runtime must validate those synthesized summaries against ground-truth environmental observations before admitting them into the prompt.

The active working context must also be decoupled from durable records stored in external backing storage. For instance, rather than inlining a verbose test log into the prompt, the runtime can provide a **raw-payload handle**\index{Raw-payload handle!definition}—a compact reference pointing to an external record that an authorized tool can dereference on demand, subject to access controls and retention policies. This architecture enforces the **handle rule**\index{Handle rule!definition}: external data enters the model's active working context exclusively through explicit, validated retrieval operations. If downstream reasoning requires a specific stack trace line or configuration parameter omitted from the initial prompt, the model can invoke a dedicated retrieval tool to bring that specific slice into the context.

Every working-set candidate must satisfy hard context admission bounds. When an inference endpoint enforces a shared context window across inputs and outputs, the serialized prompt length $\SequenceLength$ must obey the constraint $\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit$, where $\OutputLimit$ denotes the token budget reserved for model generation. When providers enforce separate input and output limits, $\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow$ applies directly. Crucially, the runtime must measure token consumption against the fully formatted wire payload—including system envelopes, chat formatting markers, and JSON tool schemas—rather than summing isolated string fragments. Because tokenizer merges and protocol framing introduce serialization overhead, token savings achieved by compressing an evidence block can easily be erased if surrounding wrappers expand.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The admission bound and the output headroom $\OutputLimit$ it reserves are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-output-headroom.
:::

While this inequality sets the global ceiling, the runtime must allocate the available token space across the distinct functional roles identified in the manifest. We model this distribution through a planning budget:

$$
S_{\text{system}} + S_{\text{tools}} + S_{\text{state}} + S_{\text{obs}} \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit.
$$ {#eq-vol3-context-budget-partition}

In this budget partition, $S_{\text{system}}$ encompasses the static system instructions, $S_{\text{tools}}$ accounts for API schemas and tool declarations, $S_{\text{state}}$ covers ongoing task constraints, historical progress logs, and active source or test excerpts, and $S_{\text{obs}}$ accommodates immediate tool execution feedback and user steering. Because these terms compete for a strictly bounded total, any expansion in one component forces an immediate contraction elsewhere. An uncurated runtime that blindly appends every raw tool observation[^fn-react-appended-observations] allows $S_{\text{obs}}$ to expand monotonically with every turn. Consequently, each new line of command-line output inexorably crowds out $S_{\text{state}}$, degrading the critical task constraints and code excerpts upon which accurate reasoning depends. @Fig-vol3-working-set-selection contrasts this unconstrained accumulation against an active selection policy: under naive append-only logging (left panel), sprawling tool outputs crowd out active state within ten turns, whereas active selection (right panel) caps interaction history and evicts stale observations to preserve a bounded working-state budget over thirty turns.

[^fn-react-appended-observations]: **Interleaved Observations**: ReAct prompting interleaves reasoning traces, tool actions, and observation payloads within an ever-expanding prompt transcript [@yao2023react]. While keeping full execution history visible simplifies early prototyping, it incurs a steep systemic penalty: the unchecked growth of $S_{\text{obs}}$ consumes prompt capacity and inflates input token costs across every subsequent inference step. \index{ReAct!appended observations}

@Eq-vol3-context-budget-partition serves as an architectural planning guide rather than an exact arithmetic identity. Because sub-word tokenization of concatenated strings does not strictly equal the sum of independently tokenized substrings, the runtime must validate the fully assembled wire payload against the provider's token limit. When the assembled request exceeds the bound, the budget partition dictates priority: it informs the runtime which component—typically the observation buffer or historical context—must be pruned or summarized. Prompt staging mechanisms order these same four components by their rate of modification to maximize prefix and KV-cache reuse.

::: {#fig-vol3-working-set-selection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Selection Protects the State Budget**: Each bar is one serialized request, stacked by the four terms of @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition beneath the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ hatched above it. Appending every tool result (A) lets $S_{\text{obs}}$ grow until it displaces the task state the next decision needs. Selection (B) keeps each term's share by moving older results into retained records outside the request, where a handle can reach them if a later decision needs them. Segment heights are schematic, not measured token counts." fig-alt="Two panels of stacked vertical bars for turns t, t plus 1, and t plus 2. Each bar stacks system, tools, state, and observation segments below a dashed input limit, with a hatched output reserve on top. In panel A the observation segment grows each turn and the state segment shrinks, turning red at turn t plus 2. In panel B the three bars are identical; an arrow moves older results from the observation segment to a retained-records box, and a dashed arrow labeled retrieve by handle returns to the bars."}
![](images/svg/context_working_set_dynamics.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-usable-context-budget
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EVIDENCE BUDGET OF A REPAIR REQUEST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition; nbk-04-evidence-budget.
# │ Goal: Show how many appended turns fit before observations overflow.
# │ Show: Evidence share, turns that fit, per-turn digest for the full horizon,
# │       and the input bill of appending vs. selecting over the horizon.
# │ How: Registry window and step budget; scenario sizes for the four terms.
# │ Note: Scenario token counts are serialized-request stipulations, not
# │       measurements of any product; bills assume no prefix reuse.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class UsableContextBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    agent = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
    window = int(agent.context_window.to(ureg.token).magnitude)  # registry window
    horizon = agent.max_trajectory_steps  # registry step budget, turns
    output_reserve = 8_000  # scenario K_max, tokens
    system_tokens = 3_000  # scenario application instructions
    tool_tokens = 12_000  # scenario tool declarations
    state_tokens = 24_000  # scenario constraints, progress record, excerpts
    obs_per_turn = 4_000  # scenario tool-result tokens appended per turn
    obs_selected = 8_000  # scenario observation share a selecting policy keeps

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    input_limit = window - output_reserve
    evidence = input_limit - system_tokens - tool_tokens
    evidence_share = evidence / window
    obs_budget = evidence - state_tokens
    turns_fit = obs_budget // obs_per_turn
    turns_fit_half = obs_budget // (obs_per_turn // 2)
    digest_max = obs_budget // horizon
    fixed = system_tokens + tool_tokens + state_tokens
    append_bill = horizon * fixed + obs_per_turn * horizon * (horizon + 1) // 2
    select_bill = horizon * (fixed + obs_selected)
    bill_ratio = append_bill / select_bill
    window_needed = fixed + horizon * obs_per_turn + output_reserve

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(turns_fit < horizon <= turns_fit_half, "Appending overflows inside the step budget; halving fits it")
    check(fixed + obs_selected <= input_limit, "The selecting policy fits every turn")
    check(window_needed > window, "The appending policy's last request exceeds the window")
    check(1.5 < bill_ratio < 3, "Appending bills roughly twice the selected input")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    window_str = fmt_int(window)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    reserve_str = fmt_int(output_reserve)
    system_str = fmt_int(system_tokens)
    tool_str = fmt_int(tool_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_int(state_tokens)
    obs_str = fmt_int(obs_per_turn)
    obs_half_str = fmt_int(obs_per_turn // 2)
    obs_selected_str = fmt_int(obs_selected)
    input_limit_str = fmt_int(input_limit)
    evidence_str = fmt_int(evidence)
    evidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(evidence_share, style="prose", precision=1)
    obs_budget_str = fmt_int(obs_budget)
    turns_fit_str = fmt_int(turns_fit)
    overflow_turn_str = fmt_int(turns_fit + 1)
    turns_fit_half_str = fmt_int(turns_fit_half)
    digest_max_str = fmt_int(digest_max)
    append_bill_str = fmt_int(append_bill)
    select_bill_str = fmt_int(select_bill)
    bill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bill_ratio, precision=1)
    window_needed_str = fmt_int(window_needed)
```

::: {#nbk-04-evidence-budget .callout-notebook title="How much of the window is evidence"}

**Problem**: In our reference repository-repair harness, an agent executes within a `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token context window under a `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget. The runtime reserves `{python} UsableContextBudget.reserve_str` tokens for generation ($\OutputLimit$) and allocates `{python} UsableContextBudget.system_str` tokens to system instructions ($S_{\text{system}}$) and `{python} UsableContextBudget.tool_str` tokens to tool declarations ($S_{\text{tools}}$). Dynamic task state—representing constraints, progress logs, and active code excerpts—consumes `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens ($S_{\text{state}}$). If every raw tool result is appended directly at `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_str` tokens per turn, how many turns fit within the window, and what maximum per-turn observation size would allow the execution to complete the entire step budget?

**Variables**: The context window and step horizon reflect the registry's repository-repair harness profile. Component sizes and per-turn observation rates represent operational stipulations for fully serialized wire requests.

**Math**: Applying @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition, the usable input capacity is `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str` − `{python} UsableContextBudget.reserve_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.input_limit_str` tokens. Deducting system instructions and tool declarations leaves `{python} UsableContextBudget.evidence_str` tokens (`{python} UsableContextBudget.evidence_pct_str` of the context window) available for state and observations. Subtracting the `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens required for state yields an observation budget of `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` tokens. Under naive appending, this budget accommodates `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` / `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_str` turns. Sustaining all `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str` turns requires constraining the per-turn observation payload to at most `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_budget_str` / `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str` = `{python} UsableContextBudget.digest_max_str` tokens.

**Result**: The appending policy exhausts the context window at turn `{python} UsableContextBudget.overflow_turn_str`, failing well before reaching the `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn budget.

**Systems insight**: The number of feasible turns is bounded directly by the observation budget divided by the per-turn observation size, making observation volume the primary design lever. Compressing each result into an informative `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_half_str`-token digest extends endurance to `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_half_str` turns, clearing the step budget. Yet context capacity is only the baseline constraint. Because an appending policy re-reads all accumulated historical tokens on every subsequent inference step, the cumulative input bill across an $\NumberOfDevices$-turn trajectory scales with $\mathcal{\Operations}(N^2)$, whereas working-set selection keeps consumption linear in $\mathcal{\Operations}(\NumberOfDevices)$. In terms of the effective cost metric $\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task), unpruned context accumulation drastically inflates the cost per accepted repair.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/ch04_append_select_bill.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two curves of cumulative input tokens from turn 1 to turn 30. A red curve labeled append bends upward; a blue line labeled select rises straight. A bracket at turn 30 spans the gap between them, labeled 2.1 times."}

*Appending re-reads every result, so its bill bends upward; selection stays linear.*
:::

The notebooks throughout this chapter reuse this baseline scenario, adopting the `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token window, the `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget, and the component token allocations defined above. These arithmetic constraints govern *admission*, ensuring that a serialized payload physically fits within the provider's context limit, but admission does not guarantee *semantic adequacy*. A prompt may strictly obey the budget yet omit the critical return path needed to formulate a patch, or conversely, it may incorporate every relevant code excerpt while burying crucial version distinctions beneath superseded error logs. Sizing a context budget is therefore only the first architectural challenge; an effective runtime must also evaluate how effectively the downstream model can retrieve and reason over the tokens admitted into that window.

## Working-Set Capacity {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics}

In notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}, the `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token window admits the investigation's complete transcript for its first `{python} UsableContextBudget.turns_fit_str` turns. Fitting an entire history within the sequence window does not mean an agent should include every interaction; utility depends entirely on what the added material contributes to the pending decision. An omitted synchronization contract will invalidate a proposed repair, whereas ten pages of repeated timeout speculation will not improve it. Raw request length cannot distinguish essential evidence from noisy distraction.

The **nominal context capacity**\index{Nominal context capacity!definition} specifies the maximum sequence length that the configured model interface physically accepts, bounded by its input and generation limits. How effectively the model reasons over a specific collection of instructions and evidence is an entirely separate question—one answered only by evaluating concrete tasks under explicit quality criteria (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set})\index{Principle!context is a selected working set}.

::: {#dfn-usable-working-context .callout-definition title="Usable working context"}

***Usable working context***\index{Usable working context!definition} is the context content, organization, and length with which a specified model and invocation configuration meet a chosen quality criterion on a stated workload.

1. **Significance**: Usable working context, rather than the nominal window, determines how much of the input allowance $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$ effectively supports decisions. It dictates how many turns an execution trajectory can sustain before selection or compaction must intervene, directly setting the input token cost per accepted task in $\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$.
2. **Distinction**: Nominal capacity is an architectural boundary of the serving interface that admits a request; usable working context is an empirical property of a task, model, and representation that only rigorous evaluation can establish.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a fixed fraction of the nominal window, or success on an isolated synthetic retrieval probe, as a universal guarantee of usable context for a production workload.

:::

For a software repair workload, that criterion might require candidate patches to pass designated regression tests while strictly honoring a permitted edit scope, with the test suite and its coverage explicitly declared. In contrast, an information extraction workload demands high precision and recall against structured schemas. Because failure modes diverge across tasks, usable context must be measured independently for each workload.

### Testing usable working context {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-usable-context-test}

An isolated retrieval probe[^fn-needle-haystack-probe] asks whether specified information can be found in an input. An agentic repair decision demands far more: the model must relate newly observed symptoms to source artifacts, preserve system invariants, and distinguish an empirical measurement from an unverified hypothesis. As @tbl-vol3-capacity-comparison illustrates, these represent fundamentally different evaluation obligations. While a synthetic retrieval probe quickly flags basic architectural blind spots, validating a runtime context policy requires decision-level verification under realistic operating conditions.

[^fn-needle-haystack-probe]: **Needle-in-a-Haystack Probes**: The best-known isolated retrieval probe plants a short fact, the needle, in long distractor text and asks the model to return it. @hsieh2024ruler found that models scoring nearly perfectly on this probe degraded sharply as length grew on tasks that require multi-hop tracing and aggregation, and that only about half of the models tested held satisfactory performance at the context length all of them claimed to support. The gap between the probe and the harder tasks is the gap between nominal capacity and usable working context. \index{Needle-in-a-haystack!usable context}

| Test obligation           | Isolated key-retrieval probe                        | Connection-pool repair decision                                                                               |
|:--------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Identify relevant content | Return the requested planted value.                 | Find the source, test conditions, and observation relevant to the notification path.                          |
| Interpret relationships   | Match the queried key to its value.                 | Tie the failure to `r17` and distinguish the missed-notification hypothesis from the observed blocked waiter. |
| Respect task constraints  | Meet the probe’s answer requirements.               | Propose a scoped change while preserving the public API and leaving untested behavior unresolved.             |
| Establish success         | Compare the returned value with the probe’s target. | Apply the chosen candidate checks and scope criteria; report only what they establish.                        |

: **Retrieval and decision scope**: A simple retrieval probe and the running repair example test different capabilities. {#tbl-vol3-capacity-comparison tbl-colwidths="[23,29,48]"}

Context organization directly influences task success even when all required facts are present in the prompt. Evaluating multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, @liu2024lost reported marked sensitivity to the position of relevant information across model architectures, with accuracy dropping substantially when key facts appeared in the middle of the input. This position sensitivity, known as **lost in the middle**\index{Lost in the middle!definition}, means systems engineers cannot treat context as an unordered bag of tokens. Placement policies must be validated against the target workload, as positional degradation profiles vary across model families and prompt geometries.

A first-order mechanism explains why appending distractor tokens cannot be treated as free. Within an individual attention head, a query assigns weight to each visible key through a softmax operation [@vaswani2017]. For a target key with scaled logit $z_{\text{target}}$ alongside $\PointtopointMessageSize$ other keys with logits $z_j = \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}_j/\sqrt{d_k}$, the target's weight is

$$
\alpha_{\text{target}} = \frac{e^{z_{\text{target}}}}{e^{z_{\text{target}}} + \sum_{j=1}^{\PointtopointMessageSize} e^{z_j}}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-softmax-dilution}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-softmax-dilution
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED-NORMALIZER DILUTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-softmax-dilution, working set capacity section.
# │ Goal: Show how fixed-logit background keys shrink one target's weight.
# │ Show: Target attention weight at two context lengths.
# │ How: Toy logits held fixed; only the number of background keys changes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import exp
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class SoftmaxDilution:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    z_target = 6  # toy scaled logit for the target key
    z_background = -2  # toy scaled logit for every other key
    short_len = 100  # total keys, short context
    long_len = 100_000  # total keys, long context

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_short = exp(z_target) / (exp(z_target) + (short_len - 1) * exp(z_background))
    alpha_long = exp(z_target) / (exp(z_target) + (long_len - 1) * exp(z_background))

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < alpha_long < alpha_short < 1, "More fixed-logit keys lower the target weight")
    check(alpha_short > 0.9 and alpha_long < 0.05, "Toy endpoints show the stated contrast")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    z_target_str = fmt_int(z_target)
    z_background_str = fmt_int(z_background)
    short_len_str = fmt_int(short_len)
    long_len_str = fmt_int(long_len)
    alpha_short_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha_short, style="prose", precision=1)
    alpha_long_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha_long, style="prose", precision=1)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_working_sets_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Line chart of target attention weight from 0 to 100 percent against the number of keys, from few to many on a log scale. The curve starts near 100 percent at a green dot and falls to near zero at a red dot."}

*Fixed-logit distractors shrink the target's share of one normalizer.*
:::

All weights share a single normalizer. Because each additional key contributes a strictly positive term $e^{z_j}$ to the denominator of @eq-vol3-softmax-dilution, expanding the sequence length while holding logits constant depresses the target key's share of attention. This structural decay is **attention dilution**\index{Attention dilution!definition}. In a toy head with a target logit of `{python} SoftmaxDilution.z_target_str` and every background logit at `{python} SoftmaxDilution.z_background_str`, the target commands `{python} SoftmaxDilution.alpha_short_pct_str` of the weight among `{python} SoftmaxDilution.short_len_str` keys. When the context expands to `{python} SoftmaxDilution.long_len_str` keys, that same target's share falls to `{python} SoftmaxDilution.alpha_long_pct_str`, even though no single background key is individually competitive.

In agent execution, this effect is often worse than unrelated filler would produce.[^fn-irrelevant-context-distraction] Stale tool executions, superseded logs, and earlier source reads share identifiers such as `waiter`, `connection`, and `timeout` with the evidence that matters. Because these semantically related tokens produce substantial inner products with query vectors, their logits remain elevated. This dynamic is a sufficient condition for dilution under fixed logits, not a deterministic forecast of failure. Production models sharpen logits, route evidence across multiple attention heads and layers, and learn position-dependent retrieval behaviors, which is why @liu2024lost measured degradation empirically rather than deriving it analytically. Furthermore, the shared normalizer causes initial tokens to act as attention sinks that absorb probability mass regardless of content [@xiao2024streamingllm]. For context selection, the architectural takeaway is direct: every staged token competes for probability mass against the evidence the next decision requires.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Why cache eviction policies must retain attention-sink tokens is developed in @sec-vol3-kvcache-intrasequence.
:::

[^fn-irrelevant-context-distraction]: **Distracting Context**: @shi2023distracted added irrelevant sentences to grade-school arithmetic problems and found that model accuracy fell dramatically, although the added text changed nothing about the answer. Because the distractors were irrelevant by construction, the drop measures interference rather than missing information. That interference is the cost an agent pays for every superseded log line and stale file read it keeps in the request. \index{Irrelevant context!accuracy loss}

### Choosing a working budget {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-working-budget}

Systems engineers size a working budget by evaluating complete context policies against representative task suites—a methodology developed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation. A context policy specifies far more than a simple token limit: it determines which material is retrieved, how structured data is represented, and where each component appears within the prompt layout. Decision quality must be evaluated alongside input size, inference latency, and token cost. Because additional context can provide essential grounding, introduce benign noise, or actively degrade reasoning through dilution, the resulting quality curve is rarely monotonic and seldom offers a single clean optimum. A documented operating envelope must therefore specify the workload, model configuration, quality threshold, and measured experimental conditions.

These decisions carry direct resource consequences under model-call cost accounting. Processing uncached tokens incurs prefill latency and compute charges, whereas aligned prefix caching amortizes prompt costs across repeated steps. High cache hit rates or discounted per-token pricing mean little if stale context degrades agent decisions. Conversely, pruning context too aggressively to reduce prefill costs risks stripping away vital constraints. Systems optimization targets meeting the task quality threshold at minimal effective cost, captured precisely by the effective cost metric $\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$ from @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task: pruning unnecessary tokens lowers the raw attempt cost in the numerator, but omitting an indispensable fact degrades the acceptance probability $\AcceptanceProbability$ in the denominator, inflating overall expenditures across failed trajectories.
In the connection-pool repair example, retaining the full transcript of early exploratory turns wastes capacity once distilled diagnostic observations, code snippets, interface invariants, and active hypotheses are available to guide the next patch. Yet stripping away a required interface contract or error log simply to compress the prompt into an arbitrary sub-budget represents a counterproductive optimization. When no evaluated policy meets both the task criterion and the available budget, the runtime must obtain the missing information, narrow the scope of the next permitted action, or report the limitation; a successful request-admission check never certifies adequate context.

Once the runtime selects the working set and bounds its token footprint, it must assemble those items into a concrete prompt layout that preserves source roles and evidence relationships while cleanly separating stable prefix content from dynamic step updates to maximize inference cache reuse.

## Staging the Next Invocation {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging}

Once a context selection policy identifies the relevant working set for an upcoming invocation, the runtime must translate those disparate entries into a concrete request payload. In our connection-pool repair task, the selected manifest contains fundamentally different classes of information: inviolable public API constraints, source code excerpts from `src/pool.py` at revision `r17`, execution results from `test_waiter_notified_on_return`, and a working hypothesis that a notification was dropped alongside an abandoned timeout conjecture. Merging these items into a flat, undifferentiated string would obscure the critical distinctions that govern the model's next decision. Staging is the disciplined process of converting selected entries into a structured request. It preserves the semantic source, authority, and revision of every item so that the model can differentiate policy instructions from empirical evidence and tentative hypotheses, while arranging content in an order that minimizes unnecessary token churn across consecutive calls.

### Ordering by change rate {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-change-rate-ordering}

A well-engineered context layout stratifies information by its rate of change, placing static material before volatile content. We partition the serialized prompt into three functional regions: the **root**, the **trunk**, and the **leaf**\index{Context zone!definition}. These zones classify content strictly by its mutation frequency during an agent's trajectory, rather than by message role or semantic authority. @Tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification maps the repair agent's selected working set into this operational order. In the running scenario from notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}, the root holds `{python} UsableContextBudget.system_str` tokens of system instructions alongside `{python} UsableContextBudget.tool_str` tokens of tool declarations. The trunk incorporates `{python} UsableContextBudget.state_str` tokens of evolving task state, and the leaf receives `{python} UsableContextBudget.obs_selected_str` tokens of freshly retained observations.

| Zone  | Contents in the repair request                                                                                           | When it changes                                                                       |
|:------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Root  | Application instructions and available tool definitions                                                                  | The application contract or tool interface changes                                    |
| Trunk | Task constraints, the current progress record, and selected source and test content at `r17`                             | A task constraint changes, an artifact is edited, or the progress record is refreshed |
| Leaf  | The latest scoped test observation and the next bounded step, here proposing a candidate change to the notification path | New evidence or a new next-step decision arrives                                      |

: **Context ordered by change rate**: The zones help preserve a stable request prefix. Message roles and source metadata remain separate from these placement choices. {#tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification}

Prefix stability must never supersede correctness. The root remains stable only as long as its specifications remain accurate; if a tool definition changes during a session, the runtime must update the root in the next invocation, accepting the cache miss. Similarly, when a candidate patch advances the repository from revision `r17` to `r18`, the runtime cannot continue staging `r17` source code simply to keep the trunk prefix warm. The earlier test failure remains valid historical evidence regarding `r17`, but verifying whether it persists on the patched workspace requires fresh execution. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot formalizes how invalidation policies govern this transition.

Information can also migrate between zones as task execution unfolds. An observation initially staged in the leaf may graduate into the trunk's summarized progress record during a planned refresh, provided its provenance, version bounds, and execution scope remain intact. Conversely, if an application instruction must be injected dynamically on a per-step basis, it resides in the leaf without forfeiting its normative authority. Zone placement dictates the physical order of tokens to optimize change frequency; structural schemas and message roles establish provenance and semantic interpretation.

### Preserving source and scope {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-source-scope}

When staging an observation, the host runtime must bind sufficient provenance metadata to interpret the underlying payload. For our failing test case, the host attaches the test identifier, the workspace revision (`r17`), the execution environment configuration, and a unique run identifier. This discipline embodies the **scope rule**\index{Scope rule!definition}:[^fn-why-where-provenance] an observation provides valid evidence exclusively for the specific artifact versions and execution conditions under which it was gathered. Every subsequent context transformation—including summarization, compaction, and invalidation—must preserve these provenance boundaries.

[^fn-why-where-provenance]: **Why- and Where-Provenance**: Database research distinguishes why-provenance, the source records that justify a result's existence, from where-provenance, the source locations its values were copied from [@buneman2001why]. The scope rule demands both for every observation: which execution and artifact versions justify its existence, and which payload spans supplied its values. A result that loses either becomes an unattributed claim that later compaction can silently generalize. \index{Provenance!scope rule}

Crucially, the runtime synthesizes this framing externally rather than extracting it from text inside the observation. A robust serializer treats raw tool output strictly as a literal data value within a structured envelope, preventing mismatched quotes, markdown delimiters, or control characters from corrupting the surrounding schema. Despite this structural isolation, the payload itself remains an **untrusted span**\index{Untrusted span!definition}: arbitrary text whose arrival the runtime can document, but whose semantic claims it cannot verify. While rigorous encoding prevents format-injection attacks, it cannot prevent the underlying language model from attending to and executing adversarial instructions embedded within the text [@greshake2023not].

Consequently, provenance labeling serves semantic interpretation rather than security enforcement. Tagging a tool output as untrusted data guides the model's reasoning, but it does not restrict the model's capabilities. If an observation instructs the agent to delete a database or overwrite production credentials, the model might still attempt that operation. Security boundaries—such as file system sandboxing, read-only workspace mounts, and deployment blocks—must execute deterministically in the host runtime, entirely outside the model's prompt interpretation. Staging maintains the architectural boundary between instructions and observational evidence, while host execution gates enforce operational safety.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The host-side information-flow policy that limits what untrusted context may influence and where private data may flow is enforced in @sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking.
:::

The proportion of untrusted tokens, their accumulation rate, and their vulnerability to staleness vary dramatically across agent architectures. A coding repair agent operates primarily over a local workspace where file contents change predictably. By contrast, an autonomous research agent ingests untrusted third-party web text at high velocity.

::: {#lhs-04-context-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Context by archetype"}

```{=latex}
\begin{minipage}{1\linewidth}
```
Each recurring workload places pressure on a distinct component of the context budget in @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition, requiring a specialized mitigation strategy (@tbl-vol3-context-by-archetype).

| **Lighthouse**        | **What fills the request**                                                                                                                                | **Binding constraint**                                                    | **Mechanism that answers it**                                                          |
|:----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Repair agent**      | Source excerpts, test logs, and a progress record from its own workspace, accumulating over a `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget | Growth of $S_{\text{obs}}$ displacing $S_{\text{state}}$                  | Compaction and progress records (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction)             |
| **Research agent**    | Retrieved pages and search results written by third parties                                                                                               | Untrusted spans that dominate $S_{\text{obs}}$ and may carry instructions | Provenance-preserving staging here; enforcement in @sec-vol3-security                  |
| **Remediation agent** | Readings of shared production state that other actors change                                                                                              | Staleness between the read and the action                                 | Invalidation and action-time preconditions (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot) |
| **Support agent**     | Fixed policy instructions and tool declarations, one customer record, a short session                                                                     | $S_{\text{system}}+S_{\text{tools}}$ repeated across many short sessions  | A stable root for prefix reuse (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging)                 |

: **Context by archetype**: The four recurring workloads bind on different terms of the same input budget. {#tbl-vol3-context-by-archetype tbl-colwidths="[16,34,25,25]"}

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}
```

**Systems insight**: The fundamental context budget equation binds on different constraints across workloads: token accumulation for the repair agent, provenance tracking for the research agent, temporal freshness for the remediation agent, and prefix cache amortization for the customer support agent. Engineering techniques rarely transfer across archetypes without adaptation. Compaction algorithms that keep a software repair agent within its token allocation do not resolve the primary vulnerability of a research agent, whose chief challenge is filtering untrusted external input rather than managing context length.

:::

### Preserving an exact prefix {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-exact-prefix}

Request organization directly governs inference performance and operational cost in modern serving infrastructure. Serving engines equipped with prefix caching[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse] bypass redundant transformer prefill computation by reusing intermediate key-value (KV) activations for identical leading token sequences. Because causal self-attention calculates each token's key and value representations conditionally on all preceding tokens, any divergence in the prefix invalidates the KV cache for all subsequent positions. Even if two prompts share thousands of identical trailing tokens, the serving engine cannot reuse the suffix cache if a single token near the beginning has changed. @Fig-vol3-context-zones partitions context into three tiered lifecycle zones (root, trunk, leaf): Call $\PointtopointMessageSize$ establishes the initial prefix across all three tiers; Call $\PointtopointMessageSize+1$ appends observations to the leaf while preserving root and trunk cache hits; but Call $\PointtopointMessageSize+2$ mutates the trunk during compaction, terminating prefix reuse at the root boundary and forcing full recomputation across all subsequent tokens.
[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse]: **Automatic Prefix Reuse**: Serving systems such as SGLang index cached attention state by token prefix within a radix tree, allowing an incoming request that shares an existing token prefix to reuse cached KV blocks transparently [@zheng2024sglang]. Because radix tree lookups evaluate exact token equality rather than semantic equivalence, two requests that diverge on an early timestamp share zero cache entries past that offset. Layout discipline directly determines cache hit rates. \index{Prefix cache!radix tree}

::: {#fig-vol3-context-zones fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token**: Three consecutive requests follow the root, trunk, and leaf order of @tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ beyond the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$. A new observation changes only the leaf, so the root and trunk remain a reusable prefix. Refreshing the trunk to r18 moves the first changed token to the end of the root, and every later token is processed again. The figure assumes compatible cached state on the serving side; an identical prefix alone does not guarantee reuse." fig-alt="Three horizontal request bars labeled call n cold start, call n plus 1 new observation, and call n plus 2 trunk refreshed. Each bar has root, trunk, and leaf segments followed by a hatched output reserve past a dotted input-limit line. In call n every segment is marked processed. In call n plus 1 the root and the trunk at r17 are marked prefix reused, and a red dashed line labeled first changed token sits at the leaf boundary. In call n plus 2 only the root is reused, the trunk is at r18, and the red dashed line sits at the root boundary. Headers name the zones above an axis running from changes rarely to changes every call."}
![](images/svg/context_staging_layout.svg)
:::

Cache equality depends strictly on the final serialized token sequence rather than abstract application state. Serialization details—such as JSON dictionary key ordering, whitespace padding, system prompt templating, and boundary token mergers—can inadvertently mutate the token stream. For instance, byte-pair encodings (BPE) frequently merge trailing whitespace with leading characters of subsequent strings, creating different token IDs across zone boundaries. Prefix stability can therefore be verified only on the fully assembled, tokenized prompt.

An identical token prefix is necessary for cache reuse, but it is not sufficient. The serving infrastructure must still retain compatible cache blocks in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), configured for the identical model weight snapshot, positional encoding offsets, and attention mechanisms. Memory pressure, LRU evictions, or node autoscaling can purge cached state between agent turns despite byte-level request stability. While serving engines manage and evict these internal tensors, the agent runtime bears the responsibility of maintaining stable prefixes for static material while accurately refreshing data essential to the next decision.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Prefix compatibility and the retention and eviction of cached KV blocks in the serving engine are developed in @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree.
:::

Placing high-frequency metadata near the start of a request destroys prefix reuse for zero operational gain. Moving dynamic elements—such as request IDs, wall-clock timestamps, or invocation counters—into the leaf preserves prefix continuity across the root and trunk. If an application requires a timestamp, isolating it in the leaf prevents it from evicting tens of thousands of reusable root tokens. When an early field diverges, cache sharing collapses at the first differing token. The following calculation takes the extreme case, where divergence occurs at the very first token, to establish an upper bound on the cost penalty of placing volatile fields at the front of a request.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-context-layout-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE OF A CONTEXT LAYOUT ACROSS ONE TRAJECTORY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout; fallacies; summary.
# │ Goal: Compare input bills under explicitly assumed prefix matches.
# │ Show: Uncached/reused tokens, input bills, and their ratios.
# │ How: Registry step budget; zone sizes are the selecting-policy request of
# │      calc-vol3-usable-context-budget (root = instructions + declarations,
# │      trunk = task state, leaf = selected observations).
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices; retained compatible cache; no latency estimate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class ContextLayoutPrice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    agent = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
    turns = agent.max_trajectory_steps  # registry step budget, one call per turn
    root_tokens = 3_000 + 12_000  # scenario instructions + tool declarations
    trunk_tokens = 24_000  # scenario task state (constraints, record, excerpts)
    leaf_tokens = 8_000  # scenario selected observations, replaced each call
    trunk_changes = 2  # after the cold first call
    input_price = 3.00 * USD / Mtoken  # hypothetical, not a provider schedule
    cached_fraction = 0.10

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    context_tokens = root_tokens + trunk_tokens + leaf_tokens
    suffix_tokens = trunk_tokens + leaf_tokens
    total_input = turns * context_tokens
    warm_turns = turns - 1 - trunk_changes
    unstable_prefill = total_input
    stable_prefill = context_tokens + trunk_changes * suffix_tokens + warm_turns * leaf_tokens
    stable_cached = total_input - stable_prefill
    hit_rate = stable_cached / total_input
    unstable_cost = (unstable_prefill * token * input_price).to(USD)
    stable_cost = ((stable_prefill + cached_fraction * stable_cached) * token * input_price).to(USD)
    cost_ratio = (unstable_cost / stable_cost).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    prefill_ratio = unstable_prefill / stable_prefill
    refresh_ratio = suffix_tokens / leaf_tokens  # trunk rewrite vs. warm call

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(warm_turns == turns - 3, "One cold call, two trunk changes, the rest leaf changes")
    check(context_tokens == 47_000, "Request equals the evidence notebook's selecting policy")
    check(refresh_ratio == 4, "A trunk rewrite costs four leaf-only calls")
    check(3 < cost_ratio < 3.5, "Unstable layout bills a little over three times the stable one")
    check(stable_prefill + stable_cached == total_input, "Every input token is billed once")
    check(0 < stable_cost < unstable_cost, "The assumed discount must reduce this input bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    turns_str = fmt_int(turns)
    root_tokens_str = fmt_int(root_tokens)
    trunk_tokens_str = fmt_int(trunk_tokens)
    leaf_tokens_str = fmt_int(leaf_tokens)
    trunk_changes_str = fmt_int(trunk_changes)
    warm_turns_str = fmt_int(warm_turns)
    price_str = fmt_usd(input_price * Mtoken, precision=0)
    cached_fraction_pct_str = fmt_percent(cached_fraction, style="prose", precision=0)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    total_input_str = fmt_int(total_input)
    prefill_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{context_tokens:,} + {trunk_changes} \times {suffix_tokens:,} + {warm_turns} \times {leaf_tokens:,} = {stable_prefill:,}"
    )
    stable_cached_str = fmt_int(stable_cached)
    hit_rate_pct_str = fmt_percent(hit_rate, style="prose", precision=1)
    unstable_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(unstable_cost, precision=2)
    stable_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(stable_cost, precision=2)
    unstable_turn_usd_str = fmt_usd(unstable_cost / turns, precision=3)
    stable_turn_usd_str = fmt_usd(stable_cost / turns, precision=3)
    cost_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio, precision=1)
    prefill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(prefill_ratio, precision=1)
    suffix_tokens_str = fmt_int(suffix_tokens)
    refresh_int_str = fmt_int(refresh_ratio)
```

::: {#nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout .callout-notebook title="Pricing a context layout across one trajectory"}

**Problem**: The repair agent of notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget} runs its full `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.turns_str`-turn step budget under the selecting policy, executing one call per turn. Each request carries a `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.root_tokens_str`-token root of instructions and tool declarations, a `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_tokens_str`-token trunk of task state, and an `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.leaf_tokens_str`-token leaf of selected observations, measured after serialization. The leaf is replaced on each call rather than appended. The trunk is rewritten on `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_changes_str` calls after the first. Input tokens cost a hypothetical `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.price_str` per million tokens, with cached reads billed at `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.cached_fraction_pct_str` of that price. What input bill follows from each layout?

**Variables**: Both layouts have `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.context_tokens_str` tokens per request and `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.total_input_str` input tokens across the trajectory, matching the selecting policy budget from notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}. In the unstable layout, the first token differs on every invocation and no prefix is reused. In the stable layout, the first call is cold; the `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.trunk_changes_str` trunk rewrites first differ immediately after the root; and the remaining `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.warm_turns_str` calls first differ immediately after the trunk. Compatible cached state remains available for every matching prefix. This calculation isolates input token pricing, omitting generation charges and cache storage fees.

**Math**: The unstable layout processes all input without reuse, incurring `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.unstable_cost_usd_str`. In the stable layout, the initial cold call processes the entire request, each trunk rewrite prefills only the trunk and leaf, and every warm call processes only the leaf. The total uncached volume is `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.prefill_math` tokens. The remaining `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_cached_str` tokens hit the prefix cache, achieving an aggregate cache hit rate of `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.hit_rate_pct_str`. Billing uncached tokens at full price and reused tokens at the reduced rate yields `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_cost_usd_str` for the trajectory.

**Result**: Average input cost drops from `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.unstable_turn_usd_str` per call in the unstable layout to `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.stable_turn_usd_str` in the stable layout. An unstable layout bills `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.cost_mult_str` the stable layout and requires `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.prefill_mult_str` times more uncached prefill tokens. These figures represent billing and token volume ratios, not end-to-end execution speedups.

**Systems insight**: With a stable prefix, the size of the volatile leaf determines the marginal input cost of each invocation. Rewriting the trunk requires prefilling `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.suffix_tokens_str` tokens—equivalent to the prefill overhead of `{python} ContextLayoutPrice.refresh_int_str` leaf-only calls. Systems engineers should place all per-call dynamic fields strictly in the leaf and restrict trunk rewrites to moments when underlying workspace artifacts or active task constraints change. This layout reduces the input component of attempt cost within the effective cost equation $\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$ by the ratio above. Task accuracy ($\AcceptanceProbability$) remains intact only as long as staged context remains faithful to real environment state: preserving a high cache hit rate never justifies retaining stale context.

:::

::: {#chk-04-context-hierarchy .callout-checkpoint title="Checking the staged request"}

A candidate patch has just moved the workspace from `r17` to `r18`, and the runtime is staging the next request.

- [ ] **Provenance after promotion**: If a test result moves from the leaf into a refreshed progress record, what source, version, and scope must remain attached to it?
- [ ] **Volatile fields**: Why does a changing field near the start shorten prefix reuse without necessarily eliminating it, and where should a per-call request identifier go?
- [ ] **Trunk refresh estimate**: With the layout notebook's zone sizes, how many uncached input tokens does the trajectory pay if the trunk is rewritten on every fourth call after the first instead of twice? Compare the result with the unstable layout's count.
- [ ] **Stale trunk**: After the source changes from `r17` to `r18`, why is keeping the old source in the trunk an incorrect optimization even when it raises the hit rate?

:::

Staging ensures that selected evidence enters the prompt in an interpretable schema and an order engineered for prefix cache reuse. However, ordering alone does not compress verbose outputs; an oversized test log or sprawling source file still consumes its full allocation of the token budget. When the required working set exceeds available context limits, the runtime must alter the underlying representation to preserve key decision evidence within fewer tokens. That compression challenge motivates compaction.

## Context Compaction {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction}

A multi-turn task such as our connection-pool repair rapidly accumulates repeated source listings, boilerplate test setup output, and sprawling execution traces. Retaining every line in every prompt consumes capacity that downstream reasoning steps need for patch analysis and test verification. Yet aggressively compressing that trace into a generic note like “the test failed” discards vital diagnostic clues: the model loses track of which source revision failed, which thread interleaving was executed, and which specific assertion triggered the timeout. Compaction must compress the working context without corrupting or discarding the causal evidence that future decisions depend on.

::: {#dfn-context-compaction .callout-definition title="Context compaction"}

***Context compaction***\index{Context compaction!definition}\index{Working-set decision!compaction} replaces material in a working context with a shorter representation chosen for the task's next decisions.

1. **Significance**: It creates room for new observations inside the fixed input allowance $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$, allowing an agent trajectory to run past the turn at which appending would overflow while retaining critical evidence, constraints, and unresolved obligations.
2. **Distinction**: A compressed representation is inherently lossy or access-deferred. Keeping a handle to omitted material makes recovery conditional on an explicit retrieval step.
3. **Common pitfall**: Assuming that a deterministic extractor, or a summary mentioning all required field names, guarantees that no decision-critical information was lost.

:::

### Choosing a compaction method {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction-method}

No single compaction strategy fits all runtime data; every representation forces a trade-off between prompt compression, downstream validation overhead, and the risk of silent information loss. A regular expression provides deterministic filtering, but it can easily drop the single line that explains an intermittent fault. A source-code skeleton preserves API signatures, yet it strips the concurrency logic needed to diagnose a synchronization deadlock. Conversely, delegating compaction to an LLM-written summary can preserve high-level diagnostic intent, but models frequently hallucinate or misstate whether a verification check actually passed.[^fn-summary-faithfulness-audit]

@Tbl-vol3-compaction-spectrum compares the choices by their preservation obligations rather than by fixed reduction ratios. The appropriate representation depends entirely on the immediate downstream operation: inspecting an interface requires only an outline, whereas debugging a race condition demands exact function bodies and thread-interleaving logs.

[^fn-summary-faithfulness-audit]: **Unfaithful Summaries**: In a human evaluation of neural abstractive summarizers, @maynez2020faithfulness found hallucinated content—statements unsupported by the source document—in the output of every model studied. A progress record written by a model inherits this failure mode. The audit developed later in this chapter therefore compares each claimed milestone with its recorded event instead of trusting the summarizer's account. \index{Summarization!faithfulness}

| Representation                    | What remains in the request                                             | What must be checked                                                                           |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Normalized or deduplicated text   | Selected text with repeated output or formatting removed                | Whether repetition, ordering, timing, or formatting carries task evidence                      |
| Tool-result digest and raw handle | Status, selected evidence, source identity, and a retrieval reference   | Whether the digest supports the next decision and the omitted payload remains accessible       |
| Deterministic extraction          | Matched log records, selected fields, source excerpts, or code outlines | Whether the extraction rule omitted relevant context, relationships, or implementation details |
| Model-written summary             | A generated account of observations, hypotheses, and progress           | Whether each retained claim is supported and required details and uncertainty remain explicit  |

: **Compaction representation choices**: Trade-offs between prompt reduction, residual prompt contents, and the downstream validation required to prevent silent information loss. {#tbl-vol3-compaction-spectrum}

The first three representation classes rely on deterministic transformations executed entirely by the runtime without invoking a language model. @Tbl-vol3-compaction-techniques summarizes these techniques alongside the failure modes they introduce. While deterministic filtering guarantees computational repeatability, it cannot guarantee semantic sufficiency; an operation is safe only when downstream decisions do not depend on the omitted lines.

| Technique                              | What it keeps                                                        | What it can silently drop                                            |
|:---------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Repeated-poll deduplication            | One copy of an unchanged status output and a repetition count        | A brief change between polls, or the timing of repetitions           |
| Terminal-control stripping             | Plain text without escape codes, progress redraws, or spinners       | Timing or ordering signals carried only by the redraws               |
| Diff hunk folding                      | Changed lines, their location, and a marker for unchanged context    | Surrounding code needed to judge whether the change is correct       |
| Superseded-read replacement            | A pointer from an old file read to the edit that replaced its source | Old text a later decision needs to explain what changed              |
| Head, tail, and failure-marker slicing | Setup lines, final lines, and lines matching failure patterns        | An intermediate warning or event ordering that matches no pattern    |
| Source outline                         | Signatures, types, and docstrings, with bodies folded                | The implementation a repair must read, such as the notification path |
| Tool-result digest                     | Status, exit code, payload size, and a handle to the retained output | Every detail of the payload until the handle is retrieved            |

: **Deterministic compaction techniques**: Specific evidence dropped by programmatic pruning methods. The trace in @lst-vol3-compaction-observation demonstrates how naive failure-marker slicing discards the causal ordering behind a test failure. {#tbl-vol3-compaction-techniques tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Lossless binary compression algorithms preserve raw bytes, but foundation models cannot reason over compressed bitstreams directly; the runtime must decompress them into natural language tokens before inference. Storing large outputs in an external artifact store and placing a lightweight digest with a retrieval handle in the context window keeps raw payloads outside the active prompt. However, paging that data back into memory costs both latency and token capacity. Under either pattern, pruned evidence re-enters the working context only through an explicit read operation.

Consider our connection-pool repair task. When executing a controlled regression test at revision `r17`, the runtime captures the log excerpt shown in @lst-vol3-compaction-observation (where repetitive polling lines have been stripped for clarity).

::: {#lst-vol3-compaction-observation lst-cap="**Observation before compaction**: The event ordering and failed assertion together identify what the controlled test observed at r17."}
```text
source=src/pool.py@r17 test=tests/test_pool.py@r17
test_name=test_waiter_notified_on_return
configuration=controlled waiter-before-return schedule
... repeated worker progress messages ...
waiter_registered_before_return=true
connection_available_after_return=true
waiter_resumed_at_notification_check=false
FAILED: assert waiter_resumed_at_notification_check
```
:::

A simplistic filter that retains only lines matching `FAILED` captures the terminal assertion failure but drops the event sequence that explains it. Without seeing that `waiter_registered_before_return` and `connection_available_after_return` both evaluated to true, the model cannot deduce whether the failure stemmed from a race during registration, an unavailable resource, or a lost notification. A structured, compact observation preserves this causal chain: “At `r17`, `test_waiter_notified_on_return` registered the waiter before returning a connection. The connection became available, but `assert waiter_resumed_at_notification_check` failed at the notification check.” Alongside this narrative digest, the context retains the revision identifiers (`src/pool.py@r17`, `tests/test_pool.py@r17`), the execution schedule, and a pointer handle to the raw execution trace for on-demand debugging.

This concise record provides empirical backing for the lost-notification hypothesis under the tested conditions while maintaining a strict boundary between raw observations and diagnostic conjectures. When a subsequent patch yields revision `r18`, the runtime must record the new test outcome against `r18` rather than overwriting or conflating it with the historical `r17` failure.
