A compaction step that collapses both runs into an unqualified summary such as “the bug is fixed” erases the provenance needed to verify that the repair actually resolved the underlying race condition.

### Protecting task-scoped fields {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-protected-fields}

To prevent compaction passes from stripping decision-critical data, the runtime designates an invariant set of **protected fields**\index{Protected field!definition} that must survive any transformation. Before committing an updated working context, the system validates that these fields are present and unaltered. In our pool-repair scenario, the protected set includes the revision identifiers (`pool.py@r17`), the test identifier (`test_waiter_notified_on_return`), the concurrent scheduling flags, the failed assertion statement, and the exit status. In addition, global task constraints—such as preserving public API compatibility, confining edits to the designated repository directory, and blocking production deployment commands—must remain pinned. Later execution stages might require specific function implementations or configuration values that this compact digest omits, but those can be paged in as needed.

Field protection must be dynamically scoped to the task phase. Pinning every historical line number, diff chunk, and identifier defeats the purpose of compaction by quickly exhausting the context budget. Conversely, enforcing an overly rigid, global schema risks dropping domain-specific diagnostic relationships. An assertion message copied verbatim without its corresponding commit hash or concurrency configuration is useless or misleading. Similarly, runtime filtering must scrub credentials, authentication tokens, and private keys; sensitive literals must never be retained simply because a filter rule matches string literals.

Furthermore, protected fields are not restricted to static configuration parameters; agents frequently uncover new invariants during execution. Suppose our concurrency reproducer fails consistently under the controlled `waiter-before-return` schedule but passes nondeterministically under the default operating system thread scheduler. The initial task specification contains no mention of this dependency; the relationship surfaces only within tool output. A naive summarizer that records “the waiter test failed” while discarding the scheduling flag permits subsequent turns to re-run tests under the default scheduler, observe an accidental pass on buggy code, and prematurely claim success. When tool feedback demonstrates that an outcome depends strictly on an experimental parameter, the runtime must promote that parameter into the protected-field inventory alongside the empirical observation supporting it. Once promoted, the parameter undergoes the same integrity checks as the original contract constraints.

Automated validation catches missing test identifiers, modified literals, or results misattributed to the wrong revision. However, validating schema conformance does not ensure that the designer selected all necessary fields or that the model will attend to them properly during subsequent decisions—concerns addressed systematically in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation. Before evicting any uncompressed payload, the runtime must assign a clear disposition to the omitted information: either it is demonstrably irrelevant to downstream tasks, it remains retrievable via an external handle, or it is permanently pruned, marking an explicit epistemic boundary. If a future reasoning step demands an evicted detail and external retrieval fails, the agent must rerun the tool or acknowledge the knowledge gap rather than hallucinating plausible execution history.

### Scheduling compaction within the request budget {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction-scheduling}

To avoid invoking compaction after every small tool observation, systems decouple the trigger threshold from the target compaction length. This dual-threshold technique, known as **hysteresis**\index{Hysteresis!compaction watermarks},[^fn-watermark-page-reclaim] allows new observations to accumulate across multiple turns before the runtime rewrites the context buffer. A narrow gap between thresholds causes frequent, expensive compaction cycles. Conversely, raising the high watermark permits longer operational trajectories between passes, while lowering the target length creates substantial token headroom by forcing aggressive compression. The optimal watermark separation reflects both token geometry and information utility: compressing too deeply risks stripping subtle evidence, while compressing too conservatively causes thrashing.

Let $S_{\text{high}}$ and $S_{\text{low}}$ denote the upper trigger threshold and the post-compaction target, respectively, measured in total serialized input tokens. Because the system must reserve capacity for model generation, these watermarks satisfy the strict inequality $S_{\text{low}} < S_{\text{high}} \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit$, where $\ContextWindow$ is the context window limit and $\OutputLimit$ is the reserved output allowance. These thresholds represent explicit runtime policy choices rather than physical model limitations.

[^fn-watermark-page-reclaim]: **Watermark Pairs**: Operating-system page reclaim uses the same two-threshold pattern. A reclaim thread wakes when free memory falls below a low watermark and stops only after restoring a higher one, allowing reclamation to run in batches rather than on every allocation. The gap balances batch size against invocation frequency, a trade-off that @eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cadence quantifies for context compaction. \index{Watermark!page reclaim}

Assuming an idealized cycle where each compaction pass resets the request exactly to $S_{\text{low}}$ and each subsequent turn appends a net volume of $\PerturnAppend > 0$ input tokens, the runtime inspects context size after each addition before issuing the next model call. The integer number of turns between compaction passes is

$$
n_{\text{cycle}} = \left\lceil \frac{S_{\text{high}} - S_{\text{low}}}{\PerturnAppend} \right\rceil.
$$ {#eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cadence}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/ch04_compaction_sawtooth.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A blue sawtooth of request length over turns 1 to 30 climbs from a dashed low line to a dashed high line, where a red dot marks each compaction and the line drops back to low. A solid red limit line sits above the high line."}

*Hysteresis turns compaction into a sawtooth whose gap sets the cadence.*
:::

Because context length is evaluated at discrete turn boundaries, the actual serialized length immediately prior to compaction is $S_{\text{low}} + n_{\text{cycle}}\PerturnAppend$. This quantity can overshoot $S_{\text{high}}$ by up to $\PerturnAppend - 1$ tokens, making $S_{\text{high}}$ a soft operational threshold. When arrival sizes vary wildly across tool calls, the runtime must either truncate individual observation payloads or stage them in a temporary buffer to prevent an unexpected payload from exceeding the hard ceiling $\ContextWindow - \OutputLimit$. Furthermore, if the runtime invokes a secondary language model to execute the compaction pass, that summarization call requires its own dedicated input and output token budgets.

Compaction interacts directly with prompt cache economics. A compaction pass that modifies the prefix trunk invalidates KV-cache reuse downstream from the rewrite point, triggering the trunk recomputation penalty modeled in Call $\PointtopointMessageSize+2$ of @fig-vol3-context-zones. For a cycle comprising $n_{\text{cycle}}$ task turns and one compaction pass, let $C_{\text{call},i}$ represent the total cost of task turn $i$ (encompassing both cached and uncached input tokens alongside generated output tokens). Let $C_{\text{comp}}$ denote the complete cost of the compaction pass under the same billing boundary. The amortized financial cost per task turn is

$$
\bar{C}_{\text{turn}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{cycle}}} C_{\text{call},i} + C_{\text{comp}}}{n_{\text{cycle}}}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cost}

Any cache misses resulting from an altered prefix are already reflected in the uncached token rates of subsequent $C_{\text{call},i}$ terms; introducing a separate cache-invalidation penalty would double-count those costs. Evaluating compaction policies requires accounting for system-level costs beyond prompt tokens, including artifact storage, secondary retrieval latency, redundant verification reruns, and trajectory failures caused by prematurely evicted context. A compaction schedule that minimizes prompt token expenditure may inflate total task cost if excessive compression forces the agent into exploratory dead ends. Runtimes must therefore optimize for the effective cost per completed task ($\CostPerAcceptedTaskEff$) rather than local turn cost $\bar{\AFourthTaxonomyAxis}_{\text{turn}}$. The watermark gap $(S_{\text{high}} - S_{\text{low}})$ directly determines $n_{\text{cycle}}$, establishing how frequently the system amortizes $C_{\text{comp}}$.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-compaction-cadence
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMPACTION WATERMARK CADENCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-04-compaction-cadence.
# │ Goal: Quantify spacing between compaction passes under stated arrivals.
# │ Show: Integer trigger cadence, overshoot, reserved output capacity, and
# │       passes within the step budget.
# │ How: Registry window and step budget; the scenario sizes of
# │      calc-vol3-usable-context-budget; hypothetical watermarks; exact reset.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class CompactionCadence:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    agent = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
    window = int(agent.context_window.to(ureg.token).magnitude)  # registry window
    horizon = agent.max_trajectory_steps  # registry step budget, turns
    output_reserve = 8_000  # scenario K_max, tokens
    low = 3_000 + 12_000 + 24_000 + 8_000  # target: the selecting-policy request
    high = 92_000  # hypothetical high watermark, serialized input tokens
    narrow_low = 81_000  # alternate target with the same trigger and arrivals
    arrival = 4_000  # scenario tool result appended per turn, tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    input_limit = window - output_reserve
    cadence = ceil((high - low) / arrival)
    trigger_length = low + cadence * arrival
    overshoot = trigger_length - high
    combined_at_trigger = trigger_length + output_reserve
    narrow_cadence = ceil((high - narrow_low) / arrival)
    narrow_trigger = narrow_low + narrow_cadence * arrival
    frequency_ratio = cadence / narrow_cadence  # passes per turn, narrow vs. wide
    passes = horizon // cadence  # passes within the step budget

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < low < narrow_low < high <= input_limit, "Ordered watermarks")
    check(arrival > 0 and output_reserve > 0, "Positive arrival and reserve")
    check(low + (cadence - 1) * arrival < high <= trigger_length, "First integer arrival that reaches the trigger")
    check(0 <= overshoot < arrival, "Overshoot is less than one arrival")
    check(combined_at_trigger <= window, "Output reserve still fits")
    check(narrow_low + (narrow_cadence - 1) * arrival < high <= narrow_trigger, "Alternate target uses the same integer trigger rule")
    check(narrow_trigger + output_reserve <= window, "Alternate reserve fits")
    check(frequency_ratio == 4, "Narrow gap compacts four times as often")
    check(passes == 2, "Two passes in the step budget, the layout notebook's two trunk rewrites")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    window_str = fmt_int(window)
    reserve_str = fmt_int(output_reserve)
    limit_str = fmt_int(input_limit)
    high_str = fmt_int(high)
    low_str = fmt_int(low)
    arrival_str = fmt_int(arrival)
    cadence_str = fmt_int(cadence)
    trigger_str = fmt_int(trigger_length)
    overshoot_str = fmt_int(overshoot)
    combined_str = fmt_int(combined_at_trigger)
    narrow_low_str = fmt_int(narrow_low)
    narrow_cadence_str = fmt_int(narrow_cadence)
    frequency_mult_str = fmt_multiple(frequency_ratio, precision=0)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    passes_str = fmt_int(passes)
```

::: {#nbk-04-compaction-cadence .callout-notebook title="Spacing compaction passes"}

**Problem**: The repair agent from notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget} appends each `{python} CompactionCadence.arrival_str`-token tool result and compacts instead of overflowing. Its `{python} CompactionCadence.window_str`-token context window, minus the `{python} CompactionCadence.reserve_str`-token output reserve, leaves `{python} CompactionCadence.limit_str` tokens for serialized input. Each compaction pass resets the prompt back to `{python} CompactionCadence.low_str` tokens (matching the baseline selecting policy's request size), and the subsequent pass triggers upon reaching `{python} CompactionCadence.high_str` tokens. How often does compaction occur, and how many passes does the agent execute across its `{python} CompactionCadence.horizon_str`-turn step budget?

**Variables**: Every compaction pass resets the prompt to the exact target $S_{\text{low}}$. Turn-by-turn additions $\PerturnAppend$ remain constant at `{python} CompactionCadence.arrival_str` tokens. The runtime evaluates buffer length after each tool addition and before dispatching the next model inference. The configured watermarks are operational policy choices rather than empirical performance limits.

**Math**: Applying @eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cadence yields $n_{\text{cycle}} = \lceil (92{,}000 - 47{,}000) / 4{,}000 \rceil =$ `{python} CompactionCadence.cadence_str` additions between successive compaction passes. The system hits the trigger at `{python} CompactionCadence.trigger_str` input tokens, overshooting $S_{\text{high}}$ by `{python} CompactionCadence.overshoot_str` tokens. Adding the reserved output capacity requires `{python} CompactionCadence.combined_str` tokens, safely within the window limit prior to compaction. Over the complete `{python} CompactionCadence.horizon_str`-turn trajectory budget, the runtime triggers `{python} CompactionCadence.passes_str` compaction passes, each incurring a prefix trunk rewrite priced according to notebook \ref{nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout}. If the post-compaction target instead rises to `{python} CompactionCadence.narrow_low_str` tokens under identical arrival rates, the operational interval collapses to `{python} CompactionCadence.narrow_cadence_str` additions.

**Systems insight**: Compaction frequency scales directly with the token arrival rate divided by the watermark gap. Narrowing that gap from `{python} CompactionCadence.cadence_str` arrivals down to `{python} CompactionCadence.narrow_cadence_str` forces compaction `{python} CompactionCadence.frequency_mult_str` as often. The per-turn amortized compaction overhead in @eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cost scales proportionally; setting a gap smaller than a single turn's arrival causes thrashing, compacting on every step. Systems designers should size the watermark gap to span multiple arrivals and compress toward $S_{\text{low}}$ only as far as protected-field constraints permit, leaving the boundary between necessary context and dispensable detail to empirical validation.

:::

A compressed observation captures only one facet of task progression. Driving an agentic repair to completion also requires maintaining the current candidate patch, the empirical checks validating it, the remaining test obligations, and the immediate next action. Because unstructured narrative summaries easily lose these dependency chains during aggressive compaction, the runtime must formalize them within an explicit, structured progress ledger.

## Structured Progress Records {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-summarization}

Consider a connection-pool debugging session that has advanced from an initial failure in revision `r17` to a candidate patch in `r18`. A naive compaction summary that claims "fixed the notification bug" discards the precise distinctions the agent needs to plan its next action. In `r17`, a controlled diagnostic test observed a released connection returning to the pool while a waiting thread remained blocked. In `r18`, a targeted reproducer passed, establishing that the waiter is now awakened under those specific test conditions. That passing check provides evidence for the patch under an isolated scenario, but it proves nothing about full regression behavior or public API compatibility. Once the raw diagnostic exchanges are pruned from the context window, the next model call must still differentiate between verified empirical observations, working diagnostic hypotheses, and a fully validated repair.

A **structured progress record**\index{Structured progress record!definition} maintains this operational state across context evictions using explicitly defined fields. Rather than replaying verbose conversational transcripts, the record encapsulates active task constraints, empirical observations, diagnostic hypotheses, artifact identifiers, and pending obligations. This schema exposes missing fields and internal contradictions to automated validation, though verifying whether those fields accurately reflect reality requires host-side auditing. This mechanism serves as a continuation record rather than an execution checkpoint: it conveys what the subsequent model invocation must know to proceed. The mechanical responsibilities of snapshotting running processes, tracking dirty workspace files, and supervising in-flight tool executions remain the domain of execution persistence.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Execution checkpoints, which bind workspace snapshots and in-flight operations to a committed log position, are developed in @sec-vol3-persistence-checkpointing.
:::

### Recording facts and open questions {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-facts-open-questions}

A reliable progress record strictly partitions objective facts that the host runtime can verify from interpretive claims generated by the model. Active operational constraints originate in the initial task specification, not in a model's fallible summary. Similarly, artifact versions and tool outcomes stem directly from host execution logs rather than free-form prose. A diagnostic narrative remains a hypothesis even when it cleanly accounts for observed symptoms. Enforcing explicit boundaries between these categories prevents a summarization step from silently mutating an exploratory directive like "test this repair" into an authoritative assertion that "this repair passed."

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The five-part task specification contract, the source of a task's binding constraints, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-five-part-contract.
:::

In the connection-pool example, the agent must not have the authority to relax public API contracts, expand workspace boundaries, or bypass deployment restrictions simply by rewording its progress record. If a human operator alters the task parameters, the runtime injects the updated contract directly instead of retaining stale instructions to preserve a prompt prefix. Consequently, every progress record explicitly references the contract version against which it was constructed, enabling the runtime to validate its contents against currently authorized constraints. @Tbl-vol3-checkpoint-schema illustrates how a structured manifest governs context continuation, defining the necessary contents and verification baselines for each field.

| Record field           | Repair information to retain                                                                                                   | Basis for checking it                                                              |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Task and constraints   | Repair waiter notification; preserve the public API; approved workspace only; no production deployment                         | Current task contract and explicit authorized updates                              |
| Artifact identities    | `src/pool.py` at `r18`, candidate patch identity, and the version of `tests/test_pool.py` and configuration used by each check | Recorded reads, applied diff, and check inputs                                     |
| Supported observations | Waiter remained blocked at `r17`; `test_waiter_notified_on_return` passed on `r18` under the recorded conditions               | Corresponding tool results, not the model's account of them                        |
| Hypotheses             | Timeout explanation lacks support from the controlled trace; missed notification is the working explanation                    | Relevant observations and a retained distinction between diagnosis and observation |
| Unresolved obligations | Broader behavior and public API compatibility are not yet established by the reproducer                                        | Required acceptance evidence compared with checks already performed                |
| Next bounded step      | Inspect the patch and relevant tests to choose the next permitted regression check                                             | Remaining task needs, permissions, and resource allowance                          |
| Raw-payload handles    | References to the original trace, patch, and test output when later inspection may require more detail                         | Retained payload identity, access permissions, and retrieval availability          |

: **A progress record for continuation**: Named fields preserve the difference between historical evidence, the current candidate, and work still needed. Field presence alone does not establish semantic fidelity. {#tbl-vol3-checkpoint-schema tbl-colwidths="[20,44,36]"}

Each observation entry obeys the scope rule: the failure observed at revision `r17` remains valuable diagnostic history, but it characterizes only `r17`, just as the passing reproducer characterizes only `r18`. Milestones must therefore record the exact operation executed and its empirical outcome rather than claiming generalized resolution. Stating that "reproducer passed on `r18`" records a verifiable event; asserting that "the race condition is eliminated" overstates what that single check proved. Similarly, the handle row implements the handle rule: whenever the agent requires an exact assertion diff or full test trace to take its next step, the runtime can fetch the raw payload through its stored reference without polluting the ongoing prompt with unneeded detail.

### Auditing before replacing active history {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-record-audit}

A model-generated progress record represents an untrusted candidate transformation of the conversation history. Before substituting this summary into the active prompt, the runtime must validate both its structural representation and its underlying claims. Schema enforcement guarantees that an observation field contains an outcome status, an artifact identifier, and an evidence pointer, but syntax checking cannot confirm that the reported outcome corresponds to an actual tool execution. The distinction between structural validity and value correctness applies as directly to context summaries as it does to tool invocations.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The gap between a schema-valid payload and a correct one is established for tool calls in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-structural-guarantee-scope.
:::

To prevent circular reasoning, the audit must evaluate candidate records against an external required-field inventory maintained by the host runtime. If the runtime trusted an internal checklist generated by the model itself, a hallucinating summarizer could omit a vital deployment constraint from both the record and its verification checklist while passing self-consistency checks. Instead, the runtime injects active constraints directly from the task specification and compares artifact hashes and test assertions against authoritative logs. Because this inventory is scoped to explicit task requirements, anticipating every latent detail a future step might need remains a context-selection challenge rather than an automatic benefit of schema validation.

When evaluating claimed progress, the runtime resolves every evidence pointer against the system execution log, matching the reported command, exit code, and artifact version against reality. A missing tool result must remain recorded as unknown; a failed execution remains failed regardless of whether the model frames the outcome optimistically; and a nonzero exit code indicates a crash without justifying speculative causes. Any diagnostic milestone must be supported by recorded evidence, and incomplete investigations must remain explicitly designated as open hypotheses.

Suppose a candidate record claims that the entire regression test suite passed on `r18`, yet host records show that the model only ran `test_waiter_notified_on_return`. The audit detects this factual conflict immediately and rejects the record. Broader questions—such as whether the single test provides sufficient coverage, whether edge cases lurk in unexercised modules, or whether subsequent actions comply with system policies—are managed through automated test execution and policy enforcement rather than the summarization audit itself.

Version tracking enforces the scope rule across code revisions. A historical finding may legitimately reference `r17` while the working tree sits at `r18`, but any claim describing the current state of the pool requires evidence generated directly against `r18`. The audit distinguishes cleanly between a missing historical payload, a valid historical observation, and an unverified assertion about current code. Treating all three indiscriminately as version mismatches would discard valuable diagnostic context while failing to confirm whether the present codebase actually functions.

@Lst-vol3-progress-audit collects these checks into one host-side function. It runs as ordinary code outside the model, and every value it compares comes from a source the candidate record did not write: the runtime-owned inventory, the recorded tool events, and the current workspace.

::: {#lst-vol3-progress-audit lst-cap="**Auditing a candidate progress record**: Every comparison uses evidence the summarizer did not produce. An empty result permits replacement; any finding rejects the candidate."}
```python
def audit_record(record, inventory, events, workspace):
    findings = []

    # 1. Required fields: contract constraints plus promoted discoveries,
    #    such as the controlled waiter-before-return schedule.
    for field in inventory.required_fields():
        if record.value_of(field.name) != field.value:
            findings.append(("missing_or_altered", field.name))

    # 2. Claimed progress: operation, result, and artifact version must all
    #    match the recorded event, not only its exit status.
    for claim in record.milestones:
        event = events.get(claim.event_id)
        if event is None:
            findings.append(("no_evidence", claim))
        elif (claim.operation, claim.result, claim.artifact_version) != \
             (event.operation, event.result, event.artifact_version):
            findings.append(("contradicts_event", claim))

    # 3. Scope: history may name r17; a current-state claim needs support
    #    recorded at the version the workspace holds now.
    for claim in record.current_state_claims:
        if claim.artifact_version != workspace.version_of(claim.artifact):
            findings.append(("needs_current_evidence", claim))

    return findings
```
:::

When applied to our candidate record, Check 2 rejects the assertion that the full regression suite passed on `r18` because the event log documents only a single test execution. Check 1 catches any omission of the no-deployment constraint or the controlled test schedule. Check 3 allows the `r17` failure to persist as an immutable historical observation while preventing the model from presenting that diagnostic failure as a description of the current `r18` workspace.

The runtime retains all raw tool logs and source diffs until the candidate record is either validated or rejected; pruning conversational turns from the prompt context does not imply purging raw payloads from backing storage. If the audit flags discrepancies, the runtime can supply the specific failure diagnostics back to the model for a targeted correction attempt, or it can bypass the model and synthesize a minimal, verified record directly from known-good state. Because iterative repair calls consume both token budgets and wall-clock latency, the system enforces a strict retry policy capping correction attempts, tool retrievals, and execution time rather than retrying indefinitely until a model output happens to pass. If repeated retries fail to yield a verified summary, the runtime must retain a larger slice of raw context (if token capacity allows), fetch essential artifacts on demand, or abort with an explicit handoff exception. Blindly accepting an unverified summary is unacceptable in production systems, and exhausting a retry budget establishes neither factual accuracy nor operational success.

### Continuing from the record {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-record-continuation}

Once validated, the progress record anchors the next model invocation. The runtime composes the prompt by combining the active contract, the audited record, and the immediate observations or code excerpts required for the upcoming decision. Staging these segments in canonical root, trunk, and leaf order allows the audited record to reside in a reusable prompt trunk, maximizing KV-cache prefix sharing across turns until an altered constraint or new execution result invalidates it. The entire prompt assembly—including structural framing and payloads retrieved via handles—must satisfy admission bounds, reserving sufficient context capacity for model generation.

In the connection-pool scenario, the subsequent call evaluates the `r18` patch with the passing reproducer and unresolved API compatibility obligations clearly visible, without re-reading pages of discarded diagnostic tangents concerning thread timeouts. If a later debugging phase requires specific details omitted during compaction, the runtime retrieves the original artifacts through their handles or surfaces the missing evidence as an explicit knowledge gap. Compaction thus acts as a staged cache rather than an irreversible, lossy compression step: repeated compaction cycles can always consult original execution logs rather than treating earlier summaries as infallible substitutes for raw evidence.

Persisting a structured record to disk guarantees that summary state survives process crashes, but context availability alone does not render an interrupted agent fully resumable. Restoring workspace files, synchronizing git worktrees, and reconciling in-flight tool calls with indeterminate outcomes demand comprehensive execution-recovery mechanisms. Context continuation fulfills a more bounded contract: it guarantees that the next model invocation receives an accurate, verified representation of task state and empirical observations under documented operational conditions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Restoring workspace state and reconciling in-flight tool calls on resumption are developed in @sec-vol3-persistence-migration.
:::

::: {#chk-04-context-compaction .callout-checkpoint title="Continuing after compaction"}

A candidate progress record says the repair is complete, while the retained evidence contains only a passing reproducer on `r18`.

- [ ] **Evidence scope**: Which claim should the audit reject, and which historical result should it retain?
- [ ] **Constraint preservation**: How can the runtime check for a missing no-deployment requirement without relying on the summary's own checklist?
- [ ] **Missing detail**: What conditions must hold before a raw-payload handle can supply an omitted assertion to the next call?
- [ ] **Correction budget**: If each rejected record costs one more call as large as the compaction pass and the policy caps corrections at two, what is the worst-case multiple on $C_{\text{comp}}$ in @eq-vol3-hysteretic-compaction-cost, and which outcomes remain permissible once the cap is reached?

:::

A structured progress record preserves the vital technical distinctions that an agent needs to continue operating after conversational history has been pruned. However, the operational utility of these recorded observations depends entirely on whether their environmental assumptions remain valid. When a developer modifies a source file, updates a configuration, or alters a test fixture, the runtime must determine which findings remain trustworthy without erasing the immutable history of what was previously observed. Reconciling active state changes with historical evidence is the core responsibility of context invalidation.

## Context Invalidation {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot}

Consider the ongoing connection-pool repair: the runtime has generated a candidate patch at revision `r18`, yet the agent's progress record still carries the failed test execution from `r17`. That failure accurately documents how the unpatched system behaved under the earlier source, test harness, and configuration. It reveals nothing, however, about whether the patched implementation in `r18` resolves the bug.

The same boundary separates historical source excerpts from active working state. An excerpt of `src/pool.py` captured at `r17` may explain why the agent formed its original missed-notification hypothesis, but planning a subsequent patch against `r18` requires inspecting the actual code at `r18`. When constructing the next model prompt, the runtime faces an explicit architectural choice: retain the earlier excerpt as immutable history, overwrite it with current source text, or evict it entirely because the upcoming decision no longer depends on it.

::: {#dfn-context-invalidation .callout-definition title="Context invalidation"}

***Context invalidation***\index{Context invalidation!definition} withdraws a staged observation's authority to support claims about current state whenever an underlying artifact or operational precondition changes, while preserving that observation as historical evidence of the state it originally recorded.

1. **Significance**: When a superseded observation leaks into a decision prompt, it introduces an unchecked step error that compounds across multi-step execution horizons (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding). Invalidation intercepts this drift by converting stale state into an explicit refresh operation scheduled before the model acts.
2. **Distinction**: Invalidation alters an observation's applicability to the present, not its historical truth. It also differs fundamentally from context deletion, which merely removes tokens from the request payload. The test failure at `r17` remains an immutable, accurate record of revision `r17`.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a fresh timestamp or an unexpired polling interval as a guarantee that an in-context observation matches the current artifact on disk.

:::

When a runtime neglects context invalidation, stale observations corrupt agent decisions through three distinct failure modes. In *offset drift*, the model plans an edit against line numbers or byte offsets retrieved at `r17`. Because the patch that created `r18` shifted the surrounding file, the patch tool rejects the edit or, worse, fuzzy-matches the hunk into an unintended function. In *ghost-symptom chasing*, the `r17` failure trace remains active in the prompt, leading the model to diagnose and attempt to repair defects that the candidate patch already resolved. In *regression from old negative evidence*, a verbose early failure log overpowers a concise passing notification from a later run; the model then unnecessarily reverts or complicates an edit that the current build actually validates. @Lst-vol3-stale-offset-edit shows how offset drift manifests at the tool execution boundary. Each failure mode conflates historical observation with current truth, a confusion that automated dependency tracking systematically eliminates.

::: {#lst-vol3-stale-offset-edit lst-cap="**An edit planned from a superseded read**: The hunk's line numbers and context come from the r17 excerpt, and the patch tool rejects it against r18. Illustrative output, not a recorded trace."}
```text
--- a/src/pool.py   (hunk planned from the r17 excerpt)
+++ b/src/pool.py
@@ -87,3 +87,4 @@
     def release(self, conn):
         self._idle.append(conn)
+        self._wake_one_waiter()
         return None
error: hunk 1 does not apply at line 87 of src/pool.py (r18)
error: expected context 'def release(self, conn):', found a different function
```
:::

### Tracking claim dependencies {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-claim-dependencies}

An observation requires rigorous provenance describing both its physical origin and the operational conditions under which it was collected. For a source code excerpt, this provenance includes the file path, repository revision, and specific line span or abstract syntax tree (AST) symbol. For a test execution, it encompasses the exact commit hash of the source, the revision of the test suite, the selected test case, runtime environment variables, and the exit status. Timestamps capture only temporal sequence; establishing what was observed requires tying the data directly to immutable content identifiers.

Derived conclusions inherit dependencies directly from their supporting observations. When the candidate patch generated `r18`, the hypothesis regarding missed thread notifications rested solely on traces collected at `r17` rather than representing an invariant fact about the codebase. Consequently, the actual runtime behavior of the patched implementation became an open question requiring fresh experimental validation. @Tbl-vol3-context-tracking-schemas details how the context manifest treats each entry following the patch.

| Manifest entry                       | Relevant dependencies                                                      | Treatment after the candidate patch                                       |
|:-------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source excerpt used to plan the edit | `src/pool.py` at the recorded revision                                     | Re-read the needed region at `r18` before planning another edit.          |
| Controlled waiter/return failure     | Source, test, and configuration used at `r17`                              | Retain as historical evidence; do not report it as a test of `r18`.       |
| Missed-notification hypothesis       | The `r17` source and observed failure                                      | Keep its status as a hypothesis; reassess using the patch and new checks. |
| Subsequent passing reproducer        | `r18`, the executed `tests/test_pool.py`, selected test, and configuration | Record this bounded result; broader behavior remains unresolved.          |

: **Dependencies and current applicability**: Each entry has a different reason to remain in, leave, or be refreshed within the repair's next request. {#tbl-vol3-context-tracking-schemas tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

The runtime maintains this manifest deterministically rather than delegating bookkeeping to model attention. Every staged observation $o$ binds to its target artifact through an **observation binding**\index{Observation binding!definition}:

$$
\FittedSensitivity(o) = \langle \text{artifact}, \text{kind}, \text{revision}, \text{range}, \text{content id} \rangle,
$$ {#eq-vol3-observation-binding}

where $\FittedSensitivity(o)$ records the artifact identifier, its type (such as a source file, test execution, daemon process, or build artifact), the revision observed, the specific byte range or symbol queried, and a cryptographic hash of the content ingested. Derived entries—including diagnostic hypotheses and test summaries—maintain directed edges to each underlying observation. Together, these bindings and edges construct an in-memory dependency graph.[^fn-truth-maintenance-system] When a tool write mutates an artifact, the runtime flags all directly bound observations as historical, traverses the outgoing edges, and marks every downstream conclusion for reassessment. Applying this graph propagation at the `r18` patch produces the lifecycle decisions in the right-hand column of @tbl-vol3-context-tracking-schemas: the `r17` excerpt and test trace transition to historical status, the working hypothesis is flagged for re-evaluation, while independent observations retain validity. @Fig-vol3-invalidation-graph traces this targeted dependency invalidation: when mutating \texttt{src/pool.py} from \texttt{r17} to \texttt{r18}, directed edges mark only dependent source excerpts and test traces as historical, flagging the missed-notification hypothesis for reassessment while leaving unrelated documentation nodes untouched.

[^fn-truth-maintenance-system]: **Truth Maintenance**: @doyle1979truth introduced truth maintenance systems to record explicit justifications for each belief held by a reasoning engine, automatically retracting beliefs when underlying premises fail. Context invalidation adopts this classic architecture for staged context windows. By delegating justification edges to the runtime graph rather than relying on model recall, invalidating stale claims reduces to a deterministic graph traversal. \index{Truth maintenance system!invalidation}

::: {#fig-vol3-invalidation-graph fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Invalidation Follows Recorded Dependencies**: Each staged observation carries the binding $\FittedSensitivity(o)$ of @eq-vol3-observation-binding, and each derived entry holds an edge to the observations it depends on. When the patch writes src/pool.py from r17 to r18, propagation marks the source excerpt and the controlled test run historical and flags the missed-notification hypothesis for reassessment. The documentation excerpt and the note derived from it keep their status because nothing they depend on changed. A historical observation remains evidence about r17; the marking removes only its support for claims about r18." fig-alt="Three columns of boxes connected by arrows. Left, workspace artifacts: src/pool.py marked patch writes r17 to r18, tests/test_pool.py unchanged, and docs/pool.md unchanged. Middle, staged observations with binding tuples: o1 source excerpt and o2 controlled test run, both badged historical, and o3 documentation excerpt badged unchanged. Right, derived entries: missed-notification hypothesis badged reassess, and API usage note badged unchanged. Red arrows run from src/pool.py to o1 and o2 and from o1 and o2 to the hypothesis; gray arrows connect the unchanged items."}
![](images/svg/ch04-invalidation-graph.svg)
:::

A dependency record makes invalidation selective. Modifying an unrelated documentation file leaves execution traces applicable to the unchanged binary or script. Conversely, editing a test assertion, adjusting a timeout configuration, or altering the core data structure immediately invalidates dependent execution claims. Whenever dependency edges are ambiguous or coarse-grained, safety dictates conservative over-invalidation: marking a broader set of entries for refresh avoids reasoning over silent regressions, because an unrecorded dependency does not guarantee freshness.

Cryptographic content identifiers verify whether input artifacts remain identical across execution steps.[^fn-build-content-hashes] When validating a derived result, the runtime compares the current content hashes of its direct dependencies against their recorded values at execution time. Even with perfectly stable inputs, nondeterministic software behaviors (such as thread interleaving or network timeouts) mean that a single passing test run remains merely a sample of system behavior. The runtime's manifest must therefore track artifact identities, spatial observation scopes, and empirical uncertainty as distinct metadata dimensions.

[^fn-build-content-hashes]: **Timestamps vs. Content Hashes**: Classic Make determines rebuild targets by comparing filesystem modification timestamps [@feldman1979make]. Consequently, touching a file without altering its contents triggers unnecessary rebuilds, whereas moving a timestamp backward can mask genuine modifications. Modern build engines resolve this by recording cryptographic hashes of input contents, rebuilding artifacts only when a dependency hash diverges [@mokhov2018build]. Context runtimes face the identical trade-off: timestamps record when an inspection occurred, but content hashes confirm whether the underlying artifact remains unchanged. \index{Build system!content hashes}

### Detecting change and bounding uncertainty {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-change-detection}

The most direct signal of state mutation is a verified write executed through a runtime tool. When a file-editing tool successfully writes `r18`, the runtime immediately marks all `r17` source excerpts as historical and registers pending test obligations for the updated code. Tool invocations that fail or raise exceptions alter nothing on disk; the runtime must verify tool exit statuses and inspect return payloads before updating dependency states. Furthermore, state tracking must reside in the runtime's authoritative metadata graph, never in conversational prompt nudges that urge the model to remember what changed.

External processes can also mutate the workspace behind the runtime's back. Inexpensive filesystem metadata—such as file size and modification timestamps—provides lightweight heuristics suggesting a refresh, but authoritative validation requires inspecting content hashes or cryptographic commit identifiers. Kernel-level filesystem watchers (such as Linux's `inotify` subsystem) reduce change-detection latency, yet queue overflows, unmonitored mount boundaries, and dropped events can silently leave a cached view stale [@linuxManpages2026inotify]. Robust runtimes treat watcher events as hints to trigger revalidation rather than as infallible event streams.

To bound uncertainty over dynamic external resources, runtimes often configure a **time-to-live**\index{Time-to-live!definition} (TTL) policy that forces a fresh read after an observation exceeds a specified duration. A TTL operates as an operational heuristic calibrated to the environment's volatility and the cost of acting on stale data, rather than as a formal proof of correctness.[^fn-lease-cache-consistency] An observation younger than the TTL window can become invalid microseconds after retrieval, while an expired observation may reflect perfectly static content. For mission-critical actions, the runtime must bypass TTL caches entirely and perform an eager, synchronous read.

Even when the runtime refreshes context immediately before generating a prompt, an unavoidable race window remains: the external system can mutate between prompt construction and tool execution. Context engineering cannot close this window in the model's token space. Guarding against concurrent mutation requires execution-time preconditions at the tool boundary—such as atomic compare-and-swap operations or optimistic revision checks.[^fn-optimistic-commit-validation] The context assembly layer's responsibility is to record the exact revision identifier on which the model's generated plan rests, allowing the tool execution layer to validate that precondition before committing destructive changes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Execution-time preconditions enforced as atomic conditional updates at the tool boundary are operationalized in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-conditional-updates.
:::

[^fn-lease-cache-consistency]: **Leases**: @gray1989leases converted temporal bounds into formal consistency guarantees through leases. In a distributed cache, a lease grants a client exclusive or shared read rights over a datum for a fixed term, during which the server guarantees it will not permit conflicting writes until every lease expires or is explicitly released. This guarantee hinges on server-coordinated consensus. Because standard filesystems and external web services provide no such cooperative write locks to an agent runtime, a local observation TTL remains a purely speculative heuristic. \index{Lease!cache consistency}

[^fn-optimistic-commit-validation]: **Optimistic Validation**: In optimistic concurrency control, transactions execute reads and computations without acquiring locks, validating prior to commit that no conflicting transaction mutated their read set [@kung1981optimistic]. If the validation check fails, the transaction aborts. Preconditions at the agent tool boundary follow this exact structure: the assembled prompt supplies the version snapshot the model evaluated, and the tool runner verifies that version's integrity before applying side effects to disk. \index{Optimistic concurrency control!action preconditions}

### Removing, replacing, or appending {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-invalidation-choice}

Once an observation no longer validates a claim about current state, the runtime must decide how to represent that invalidation in the subsequent prompt. @Tbl-vol3-invalidation-policies contrasts three fundamental strategies: evicting the outdated payload entirely, replacing it in place with a lightweight tombstone or fresh read, or appending an advisory notice to the end of the context. These strategies govern both what the model perceives and how much of the prompt can leverage the KV-cache prefix.

| Policy                      | What the next request contains                                                               | Limitation                                                                                              |
|:----------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Remove the old payload      | Other selected material, without the outdated excerpt                                        | The request no longer supplies that historical detail; provenance must be retained elsewhere if needed. |
| Replace the old payload     | Current evidence, or a short marker that identifies the superseded entry and pending refresh | A marker is not fresh evidence; changing earlier tokens also changes the reusable prefix boundary.      |
| Append a superseding notice | The unchanged old payload plus a notice describing its status                                | The outdated material remains visible and occupies capacity; the notice does not enforce correct use.   |

: **Invalidation representation choices**: Removing a payload, replacing it in place, and appending a notice are different operations, even when each is described informally as tombstoning, the practice of leaving a marker where deleted content stood. {#tbl-vol3-invalidation-policies tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

In the connection-pool scenario, an in-place replacement marker can state explicitly that the previously displayed source belongs to `r17` and that the agent must inspect `r18` before attempting another edit. If the earlier test failure provides valuable diagnostic history, the runtime can retain a compact summary of that failure alongside the pending check status. This architecture maintains the continuity of the investigation without misrepresenting stale code as current reality; storing a handle to the full `r17` excerpt preserves auditability without wasting working-set capacity.

Appending an advisory notice to the prompt conserves the KV-cache prefix across turns, but it forces the model to arbitrate between the original payload and the superseding correction.[^fn-tombstone-storage-engines] Merely placing the notice at the end of the context or emphasizing it with system directives provides no architectural guarantee that attention will prioritize the update over the vivid, detailed error text above it. Conversely, outright payload deletion purges the raw tokens but risks leaving orphan hypotheses or derived conclusions intact unless the runtime explicitly propagates retraction across the dependency graph. Both payload removal and in-place replacement invalidate the KV-cache prefix at the point of mutation: because prefix caching matches token sequences from left to right, altering even a single token forces the inference engine to recompute the entire subsequent suffix, regardless of whether the token count changed.

[^fn-tombstone-storage-engines]: **Tombstones in Storage Engines**: Log-structured storage engines like Bigtable record deletions by writing tombstones, which actively mask superseded values during read scans until major compaction discards both the tombstone and the deleted record [@chang2008]. The storage engine's read path mechanically enforces this masking. In contrast, an appended advisory notice in a language model prompt enjoys no mechanical read filter: the superseded text remains fully visible in the attention matrix, leaving the model to heuristically resolve the contradiction. \index{Tombstone!storage engines}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: context-invalidation-tokens
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TOKEN ACCOUNTING FOR INVALIDATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-04-invalidation-tokens; fallacies.
# │ Goal: Account for request residency and nonreused suffixes after invalidation.
# │ Show: Resident tokens and tokens beyond the reusable prefix for removing,
# │       replacing, or appending.
# │ How: The selecting-policy request of calc-vol3-usable-context-budget; the
# │      excerpt opens the trunk, so the reusable prefix is the root.
# │ Note: Excerpt, marker, and notice sizes are hypothetical serialized counts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class ContextInvalidationTokens:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    original = (3_000 + 12_000 + 24_000 + 8_000) * count  # selecting-policy request
    prefix = (3_000 + 12_000) * count  # root: instructions + tool declarations
    old_excerpt = 850 * count  # superseded r17 excerpt at the start of the trunk
    marker = 24 * count
    notice = 128 * count

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Unchanged other content; no new read or output included.
    removed_total = original - old_excerpt
    removed_suffix = removed_total - prefix
    replaced_total = removed_total + marker
    replaced_suffix = replaced_total - prefix
    appended_total = original + notice
    appended_suffix = notice
    suffix_ratio = (replaced_suffix / appended_suffix).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(prefix + old_excerpt < original, "Excerpt must precede a retained suffix")
    check(removed_total + old_excerpt == original, "Removal must subtract the excerpt")
    check(removed_suffix + prefix == removed_total, "Removed request must balance")
    check(replaced_suffix + prefix == replaced_total, "Replaced request must balance")
    check(appended_suffix + original == appended_total, "Appended request must balance")
    check(removed_suffix == 31_150 * count, "Removal suffix must exclude 850 old tokens")
    check(replaced_suffix == 31_174 * count, "Replacement includes the 24-token marker")
    check(200 < suffix_ratio < 300, "Replacement reprocesses a few hundred times the notice")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    original_str = fmt_tokens(original)
    old_excerpt_str = fmt_tokens(old_excerpt)
    prefix_str = fmt_tokens(prefix)
    marker_str = fmt_tokens(marker)
    notice_str = fmt_tokens(notice)
    removed_total_str = fmt_tokens(removed_total)
    removed_suffix_str = fmt_tokens(removed_suffix)
    replaced_total_str = fmt_tokens(replaced_total)
    replaced_suffix_str = fmt_tokens(replaced_suffix)
    appended_total_str = fmt_tokens(appended_total)
    appended_suffix_str = fmt_tokens(appended_suffix)
    suffix_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(suffix_ratio), precision=0)  # rounded for prose
```

::: {#nbk-04-invalidation-tokens .callout-notebook title="Token accounting for invalidation"}

**Problem**: How do payload removal, in-place replacement, and appended notices alter resident token counts and the uncached suffix that the inference engine must recompute?

**Variables**: The baseline prompt is the `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.original_str`-token request configured under the selecting policy of notebook \ref{nbk-04-evidence-budget}. An outdated `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.old_excerpt_str`-token source excerpt from `r17` sits at the start of the dynamic trunk, leaving the `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.prefix_str`-token root (system instructions and tool declarations) as the unchanged prefix. An in-place tombstone marker consumes `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.marker_str` tokens; an appended advisory notice, including its role and message framing, consumes `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.notice_str` tokens. These quantities represent serialized token counts assuming isolated modifications without cross-boundary BPE re-tokenization. Removal and replacement both diverge from the baseline at the end of the root prefix, terminating KV-cache reuse at that boundary.

**Math**: Evicting the excerpt yields `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.original_str` − `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.old_excerpt_str` = `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.removed_total_str` resident tokens. Subtracting the reusable prefix leaves `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.removed_total_str` − `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.prefix_str` = `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.removed_suffix_str` tokens in the uncached suffix that requires prefill computation.

Replacing the excerpt with a tombstone leaves `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.removed_total_str` + `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.marker_str` = `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.replaced_total_str` resident tokens, creating an uncached suffix of `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.replaced_total_str` − `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.prefix_str` = `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.replaced_suffix_str` tokens. In contrast, appending an advisory notice leaves all earlier tokens untouched, yielding `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.original_str` + `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.notice_str` = `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.appended_total_str` resident tokens; here, only the new `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.appended_suffix_str`-token tail extends beyond the cached prefix.

**Systems insight**: Appending preserves KV cache locality across the turn, forcing prefill across only `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.appended_suffix_str` tokens compared to `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.replaced_suffix_str` tokens under in-place replacement—a processing difference of roughly `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.suffix_mult_str`. Yet this immediate cache savings carries high downstream interest: retaining all `{python} ContextInvalidationTokens.old_excerpt_str` superseded tokens dilutes attention capacity (@eq-vol3-softmax-dilution) and induces ghost-symptom chasing in subsequent steps. Systems architects should apply a hybrid policy informed by the dependency graph: append an advisory notice for inert historical context that the agent might cite as rationale, but decisively replace or tombstone code regions that subsequent edits target, amortizing the cost of a trunk rewrite (notebook \ref{nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout}). Because none of these three strategies fetches fresh source, the subsequent read of `r18` and the agent's output reserve must be budgeted separately.

:::

Context invalidation preserves the essential boundary between historical observation and actionable present truth. An effective runtime policy unifies deterministic dependency tracking, bounded freshness heuristics, and deliberate context representations that balance attention hygiene against prefix-cache hit rates. The primary engineering objective is empirical: ensuring that context updates supply sufficient evidence for correct, constraint-respecting actions while minimizing token expenditure and prefill latency across multi-step execution horizons. Determining whether an assembled context policy achieves that balance without silently dropping constraints or acting on stale evidence requires evaluating the complete context lifecycle under realistic task workloads.

## Evaluating Context Policies {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-evaluation}

Consider an automated software repair agent that has compacted its diagnostic history and applied a candidate patch, advancing the repository workspace from revision `r17` to `r18`. Its next model request contains the overarching task constraints alongside a diagnostic record that `test_waiter_notified_on_return` failed at revision `r17`. At this junction, the context policy succeeds only if the subsequent prompt provides sufficient evidence to distinguish the active candidate patch from the earlier failure, while identifying which verification checks remain outstanding. Token reduction alone is never evidence of success. When compaction erases version boundaries, an agent can easily mistake an obsolete diagnostic failure for current reality—or mistake a partial reproducer pass for complete task success.

::: {#exmp-04-context-evidence-probe .callout-example title="A passing test without its version"}

**Scenario**: At revision `r17`, the test `test_waiter_notified_on_return` reveals a concurrency bug: a connection becomes available while a waiting worker remains blocked. A candidate patch produces revision `r18`, and an isolated execution on `r18` passes this specific reproducer under the recorded test configuration. Broader system behavior remains unverified. Before assembling the next model prompt, a naive compaction policy replaces these detailed entries with a single summary: "The waiter test passed; the repair is complete." The original API constraints and production deployment prohibitions are preserved in the prompt text.

**Diagnosis**: A schema validator checking for a string-valued `test_status` accepts the summary without error, and a rule-based constraint check confirms that both negative constraints remain present. Yet neither check detects that a localized, single-case observation was erroneously promoted into an assertion of complete task success. An evidence probe addresses this gap by freezing the execution history and inspecting the assembled prompt and the subsequent model decision. It verifies candidate and test identities, reproducer scope, and unresolved acceptance obligations. In a controlled variant, the evaluator mutates a relevant test or source file after the passing run. An effective context policy must prompt the agent to recognize that the earlier pass no longer characterizes the mutated candidate, compelling it to collect fresh evidence before declaring victory. Conversely, an unrelated file modification provides a contrasting control where the evaluator ensures the policy does not trigger indiscriminate context invalidation.

**Systems lesson**: A context policy must preserve causal relationships and version bindings, not merely isolated field names. A test result has meaning only relative to the exact artifact and execution conditions under which it was produced, and subsequent decisions must respect those boundaries. Targeted evidence probes pinpoint semantic information loss, while repeated dynamic trials verify whether the agent acts on those preserved distinctions during execution.

:::

Every mechanism in context engineering converges on failures of this kind. Selection determines which material enters the working prompt; staging establishes representation and ordering; compaction and progress ledgers govern what survives across context boundaries; and invalidation dictates when stale support must be refreshed. Evaluating context quality by summary length alone ignores the subtle semantic failure modes that emerge at these architectural joins. Rigorous evaluation therefore demands comparing the complete context policy—including its external source retrieval, schema transforms, and fallback paths—under the operational constraints and resource limits of the target task.

### Comparing complete policies {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-policy-comparison}

A controlled comparison starts each repair trial from the identical source snapshot, task contract, and baseline observations. The evaluation harness holds the model configuration, sampling parameters, tool interfaces, and acceptance tests fixed while varying only the context policy. Each candidate policy operates under identical resource ceilings, such as the `{python} UsableContextBudget.window_str`-token window and the `{python} UsableContextBudget.horizon_str`-turn step budget of the benchmark scenario. However, identical limits do not yield identical resource consumption. A policy that executes supplementary source reads or invokes an auxiliary model for recursive summarization pays for that compute against the shared task budget.

An honest policy specification must account for operational decisions that otherwise introduce unmeasured advantages. A sliding-window policy requires an explicit retention rule for pinned system instructions and base constraints. A summarizing policy requires an explicit trigger threshold, a target compaction ratio, a protected-field schema, and defined fallback behavior when summary validation fails. Similarly, any policy that replaces raw payloads with external database handles must specify how the runtime responds to retrieval misses. Vague labels like "sliding window," "summarizer," or "structured ledger" obscure these operational mechanics, yet fallback paths frequently decide whether an agent recovers or terminates prematurely due to missing context.

Example \ref{exmp-04-context-evidence-probe} diagnoses how easily ungrounded statements can slip past inspection when the context fails to provide an unambiguous citation trail.

Repeated trials across cohorts remain essential even with greedy decoding or fixed random seeds. In distributed inference systems, model serving engines, low-level kernel non-determinism, and asynchronous environment scheduling introduce subtle run-to-run variations. Benchmark protocols must log exact model versions, serving infrastructure revisions, sampling hyperparameters, sandbox environments, and KV-cache settings. Confounding context policy changes with serving infrastructure updates obscures causality, measuring artifact shifts across the combined system rather than context selection. A single successful trajectory provides an existential proof of capability, not a reliable performance estimate.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How many tasks and repeated runs an estimate needs, and the confidence intervals on acceptance rates, are developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor.
:::

### Measuring retention, behavior, and cost {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-retention-behavior-cost}

An evaluation harness must separate an information omission in the prompt from a model's failure to attend to an available field. For every probe, define the required information schema against the task fixture before inspecting candidate outputs. In the software repair scenario, this manifest includes public API constraints, the designated workspace directory, deployment prohibitions, exact source and test identities, and the recorded scope of test executions. This inventory forms an explicit evaluation criterion, strictly bounded by the conditions anticipated in the fixture.

**Required-field retention**\index{Required-field retention!definition} measures the ratio of correctly represented required items to total required items assessed. A field counts as retained only when its value, scope, and provenance agree with the ground-truth fixture; the mere appearance of a key named `test_status` is insufficient. Exact identifiers or compiler diagnostics can be verified through deterministic string equality. Paraphrased claims, by contrast, require semantic validation rules that account for annotator disagreement or evaluation uncertainty. Diagnostic logs should categorize omitted, corrupted, and unsupported fields separately whenever those distinctions alter the systems diagnosis.

Retention across successive compaction cycles is a much stricter property than retention after a single round. An item can vanish from context during intermediate steps and subsequently reappear through an expensive re-fetch. The benchmark specification must declare whether it measures instantaneous presence at each compaction boundary, uninterrupted retention across the entire episode, or just-in-time recovery prior to decision execution. For uninterrupted retention of a critical constraint set $\TaskContract$ across $k$ compaction boundaries, the empirical retention metric is

$$
\eta_{\TaskContract}(\NoisePredictionNetworkThree = \frac{1}{|\TaskContract|} \sum_{c \in \TaskContract} \prod_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{\ArithmeticIntensity}\left[c \text{ correctly retained at boundary } i\right].
$$ {#eq-vol3-constraint-retention}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-constraint-retention
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONSTRAINT RETENTION ACROSS COMPACTION ROUNDS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-constraint-retention, context policy evaluation section.
# │ Goal: Show how a small per-round loss compounds over repeated compaction.
# │ Show: Single-item survival probability after a short and a long run.
# │ How: Hypothetical independent per-round loss; one specified item only.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class ConstraintRetention:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    loss_per_round = 0.05  # hypothetical probability one item is lost per round
    short_rounds = 10
    long_rounds = 40

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    survive_short = (1 - loss_per_round) ** short_rounds
    survive_long = (1 - loss_per_round) ** long_rounds

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < survive_long < survive_short < 1, "Survival falls with more rounds")
    check(survive_long < 0.2 < 0.5 < survive_short, "Endpoints show the stated contrast")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    loss_pct_str = fmt_percent(loss_per_round, style="prose", precision=0)
    short_rounds_str = fmt_int(short_rounds)
    long_rounds_str = fmt_int(long_rounds)
    survive_short_pct_str = fmt_percent(survive_short, style="prose", precision=1)
    survive_long_pct_str = fmt_percent(survive_long, style="prose", precision=1)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/ch04_constraint_survival.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A red curve of single-constraint survival probability falls from 100 percent at zero rounds toward zero. A green dot at 10 rounds is labeled 59.9 percent and a red dot at 40 rounds is labeled 12.9 percent."}

*A small per-round loss compounds geometrically over repeated compactions.*
:::

The product in @eq-vol3-constraint-retention demonstrates why recursive context compaction poses severe reliability hazards. When a required constraint or fact survives an individual compaction step independently with probability $1-\CommunicationcomputationRatio$, its survival probability across $k$ successive compactions compounds to $(1-\CommunicationcomputationRatio)^k$, mirroring the horizon-compounding dynamics of @eq-vol3-horizon-compounding with compaction intervals replacing raw decision turns. For example, with an apparently modest per-round loss rate of `{python} ConstraintRetention.loss_pct_str`, a constraint survives `{python} ConstraintRetention.short_rounds_str` compaction rounds with probability `{python} ConstraintRetention.survive_short_pct_str`, but survives `{python} ConstraintRetention.long_rounds_str` rounds with probability only `{python} ConstraintRetention.survive_long_pct_str`. An information loss rate that appears negligible during a single compaction benchmark quickly erodes system constraints over extended executions. This exponential decay explains why robust production systems validate protected schema fields programmatically at every compaction boundary rather than trusting an unconstrained neural summarizer. Scaling this analytical model across the complete working set requires modeling joint survival distributions, as real-world compaction failures often exhibit strong cross-field correlations within a round.

Behavioral metrics require precisely defined denominators. For example, a constraint-violation rate must measure the proportion of violating actions specifically against the subset of decision points where that constraint was applicable. Diagnostic harnesses must record proposed actions rejected by safety filters without executing them, separating generation errors from downstream enforcement failures. Similarly, the **stale-support rate**\index{Stale-support rate!definition}

$$
\StalesupportRate = \frac{\text{decisions that treat superseded support as current}}{\text{decisions that require current evidence}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-stale-support}

restricts its denominator strictly to decisions where evidence currency affects execution validity. Referencing the historical `r17` test failure remains valid and informative after the workspace transitions to `r18`; the operational failure occurs when the agent treats that past diagnostic as proof of a property in `r18` without executing fresh checks. Test fixtures and execution trace audits must codify these classification boundaries explicitly.

Task acceptance supplies the primary end-to-end evaluation metric:

$$
\hat{\HiddenDimensionFour}_{\text{acc}} = \frac{\AcceptedTasks}{\NumberOfDevices},
$$ {#eq-vol3-task-acceptance}

estimating the true acceptance probability $\AcceptanceProbability$ defined in @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task. Here, $\AcceptedTasks$ represents the count of trials that successfully satisfy the verification standard within allocated resource budgets, while $\NumberOfDevices$ represents the total cohort of assigned trials. Passing a localized reproducer test is merely an intermediate observation within that standard; it does not constitute general proof of patch correctness. Incomplete runs, policy timeouts, tool execution crashes, and context budget exhaustion must remain in the denominator $\NumberOfDevices$ rather than being silently discarded. The measurement contract outlined in @tbl-vol3-context-evaluation organizes these complementary evaluation tiers, with @eq-vol3-stale-support and @eq-vol3-task-acceptance establishing precise denominator definitions for behavioral and end-to-end evaluation.

| Measurement              | What the evaluator records                                                                     | What the result cannot establish                           |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Required-field retention | Correct values and evidence scope at each specified compaction boundary                        | That the inventory includes every fact needed later        |
| Constraint compliance    | Violating proposals among applicable proposals, separately from executed violations            | That prompt text enforces an action boundary               |
| Current-evidence use     | Decisions using superseded support as current, among eligible decisions                        | That every old observation is irrelevant                   |
| Task acceptance          | Trials meeting the common evidence standard, including every assigned trial in the denominator | Correctness beyond that standard's coverage                |
| Request footprint        | Fully serialized input length, output reservation, and rejected oversized requests             | Lower total task cost or adequate information              |
| Resource use             | All calls, source reads, compaction, checks, and elapsed time charged to the cohort            | A benefit unless accepted outcomes justify the expenditure |

: **Context-policy measurement contract**: Representation checks, behavioral observations, and task outcomes answer different questions. Their denominators and coverage must remain explicit when comparing policies. {#tbl-vol3-context-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[21,43,36]"}

Compression measures representation volume rather than decision quality. To calculate compression at a given decision step, serialize two alternative prompts using an identical tokenizer: an uncompacted reference prompt containing the complete raw history, and the candidate prompt produced by the context policy. Both serializations must include system instructions, tool declarations, structured schemas, and framing delimiters. The **request compression ratio**\index{Request compression ratio!definition} is defined as

$$
\gamma_{\text{req}} = \frac{S_{\text{ref}}}{S_{\PeakArithmeticRate}},
$$ {#eq-vol3-request-compression}

where $S_{\text{ref}}$ and $S_{\PeakArithmeticRate}$ represent the token counts of the uncompacted reference request and the policy-generated request, respectively. The uncompacted baseline $S_{\text{ref}}$ serves as an analytical reference and may exceed the context window of the model serving engine; measuring it does not require executing it. Under this formulation, values of @eq-vol3-request-compression exceeding $1.0$ indicate token reduction. Evaluators must maintain consistent token accounting across both terms: dividing raw observation tokens by a fully serialized prompt introduces measurement asymmetry and invalidates comparative analysis.

Compression ratios are also sensitive to trajectory variance. In static-trace probes where every policy ingests an identical historical trace, request lengths compare directly.
